World.title: ‘Georgia deserves better’: opposition rally on country’s Independence Day
World.content:
Opposition rally on Georgia’s Independence Day

On 26 May, Georgia’s Independence Day, an opposition rally took place in Tbilisi. The demonstration began with a march from the grounds of Tbilisi State University to the parliament building and ended on Rustaveli Avenue.

Thousands of people took part in the rally, making it the largest protest seen in recent months.

The alliance, which brings together nine opposition groups, centred its message on unified resistance to the government’s course and launched a new campaign under the slogan: “Georgia deserves better.”

The video shows the metro in Tbilisi late on 26 May 2026, as participants leave a large pro-European march held on Georgia’s Independence Day. “We will go all the way,” hundreds of people chant on the escalators.

Opposition leaders delivered speeches outside parliament.

According to Nika Gvaramia, leader of the Ahali party, which is part of the alliance, the opposition campaign will spread across the country and conclude with new democratic elections.

One of the opposition’s main demands is the release of political prisoners.

Opposition parties outside the alliance — including representatives of Lelo, Girchi and For Georgia — did not take part in the rally.

Georgia’s fifth president, Salome Zourabichvili, also joined the demonstration. She said protecting independence depends on unity.

The day unfolded amid tensions between the opposition and the authorities. Police prevented the opposition alliance from bringing sound equipment to the parliament building.

However, after the march began, organisers managed to install a sound system near parliament and address participants.

After the rally ended, police stopped a truck transporting speakers and a generator to the protest site. Officers fined the driver 1,000 lari ($375) and suspended his driving licence for one year.

Continuous protests in Georgia have persisted since late November 2024, when the ruling Georgian Dream party suspended the country’s European Union accession process.

Opposition rally on Georgia’s Independence Day

World.title: National Bank of Georgia: ‘Georgian companies sanctioned by UK were not under our supervision’
World.content:
National Bank of Georgia on sanctioned companies

The National Bank of Georgia said three Georgian companies sanctioned by the UK over alleged involvement in helping Russia circumvent sanctions do not fall under the regulator’s supervision.

The bank explained that the companies operated without registration and, as a result, the National Bank had no supervisory authority over them.

The National Bank also said that when it identifies unauthorised activity, it cooperates with law enforcement agencies and has already provided relevant information in this specific case.

According to the National Bank, in September 2025 it provided law enforcement agencies with information on organisations operating without registration and “applied appropriate supervisory measures”.

The bank also says that, based on information available to it, investigations into these cases are ongoing and that authorities have established responsibility in some instances.

In its statement, the National Bank stresses that Georgia’s regulatory framework for virtual asset service providers complies with international standards.

The regulator also refers to a 2024 assessment by the Council of Europe’s Committee of Experts on the Evaluation of Anti-Money Laundering Measures, which found that Georgia is “largely compliant” with FATF Recommendation 15 (meaning the recommendation has been substantially implemented, with only minor or moderate shortcomings — JAMnews).

According to the National Bank, the UK and France have received the same assessment.

Context

The National Bank of Georgia issued its statement after the UK expanded its sanctions against Russia and added three Georgian companies to the list.

The British government said the new package of measures aims to restrict cryptocurrency networks and shadow financial systems that Moscow uses to circumvent international sanctions.

Among the sanctioned entities is Tbilisi-registered AIFORY LLC, which the UK government accuses of supporting Russia’s financial sector. The sanctions will restrict the company’s banking operations and payment processing.

According to business registry records, Giorgi Nutsubidze registered the company in June 2023. Its legal address is in the Tbilisi Free Industrial Zone on Omar Khizanishvili Street.

Authorities registered ARVIX LLC at the same address. According to the UK government, the company had links to Russian cryptocurrency exchanges Garantex and Grinex.

Under the sanctions, ARVIX will face restrictions related to internet services. Business registry records show that Davit Nutsubidze founded the company in October 2023.

The sanctions list also includes RAPIRA GROUP LLC, which London says provided financial services to the Russian government, thereby undermining Ukraine’s territorial integrity.

The company is registered in Kutaisi, and Ilya Akhaev is listed as its founder. Under the UK government’s decision, the company will face restrictions on banking operations and payment processing.

National Bank of Georgia on sanctioned companies

World.title: ‘Creating a new path’ – Marco Rubio on agreements signed in Yerevan
World.content:
Marco Rubio in Yerevan

Armenia and the United States initialled a framework agreement on strategic cooperation around the TRIPP project (Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity). The initiative envisions a transport route linking Azerbaijan with its exclave of Nakhchivan while also contributing to the unblocking of transport links across the wider region. The signing took place during Marco Rubio’s visit to Yerevan, where he arrived together with his wife.

“It is a pleasure to be here to continue advancing the concept and vision of President Trump and Prime Minister Pashinyan — this bold path towards peace in the South Caucasus,” the US secretary of state said. He also recalled that the foundations for the peace process had been laid during the Washington summit on 8 August 2025.

Marco Rubio and Armenian Foreign Minister Ararat Mirzoyan also signed two additional documents:

a charter “On Comprehensive Strategic Partnership between Armenia and the United States”;

a framework memorandum “On Securing Supply Chains in the Extraction and Processing of Critical Minerals and Rare Earth Elements”.

Following the signing ceremony, the two officials delivered statements to the press.

Ararat Mirzoyan stressed that Armenia-US strategic partnership had reached a new level. According to him, the agreements reached are “clearly beneficial for Armenia and will open unprecedented opportunities”. He added that relations between Armenia and the United States are now stronger than ever before.

The Armenian foreign minister also thanked the US secretary of state for “finding time in his busy schedule” to visit Armenia.

“This highly substantive visit demonstrates the unwavering commitment of both Yerevan and Washington to consistently strengthening our bilateral ties,” he said.

Expanded-format Rubio-Mirzoyan talks, the signing ceremony and the press briefing all took place directly at Zvartnots International Airport. Roughly an hour after arriving in Yerevan, the US secretary of state’s visit concluded.

After seeing off his counterpart, Ararat Mirzoyan continued speaking to journalists during a separate press conference, where he outlined further details of the signed agreements.

Marco Rubio: “Our cooperation is not limited to TRIPP”

The US secretary of state made the following statements:

US-Armenia cooperation is not limited to the Trump Route project. The two sides continue to expand cooperation across multiple areas.

The Comprehensive Strategic Partnership Charter defines the framework for bilateral relations and charts a new path that will benefit both Armenians and Americans.

Both countries should see the benefits of their deepening ties. A partnership becomes strategic when the sides share a vision for the future and can help one another achieve it.

The extraction and processing of minerals are essential for future prosperity. Countries capable of developing these sectors will be able to achieve economic independence and position themselves at the centre of 21st-century innovation.

The United States and Armenia can work together to ensure that both countries and both economies have secure access to critical minerals.

Key Takeaways from Ararat Mirzoyan’s Press Conference

TRIPP agreement to be signed within weeks

The Armenian foreign minister said that all three signed documents were “equally important”. However, he stressed that progress on the agreement related to the implementation of the TRIPP project had long been anticipated.

“The initialling will very soon lead to the signing stage. The text has been fully agreed, and there is political understanding and consensus. There are simply technical procedures that still need to be completed in both countries.”

He explained that there are also other documents linked to the Trump Route project that are not yet ready. In particular, work on the charter has not yet been finalised.

Mirzoyan said he expects all outstanding issues to be resolved within several weeks, after which the agreement will be signed and work on the ground will begin.

“Both the US administration and the Armenian government are working intensively on this project. They attach great importance to the implementation of TRIPP, even amid the current geopolitical, regional and highly active domestic political environment. And this is happening against the backdrop of speculation that the United States has supposedly lost interest in the project.”

Involvement of Russia, Iran and other countries in TRIPP

Journalists asked whether concerns and dissatisfaction in Moscow and Tehran could hinder the implementation of the Trump Route project. The Armenian foreign minister replied that the government in Yerevan was familiar both with the official positions of those countries and with expert assessments.

He stressed that officials in Iran had previously expressed concerns about the project’s “security component”. However, according to him, those concerns faded after the relevant documents were published. He added that any remaining questions could also be addressed once the documents are reviewed.

“In any case, questions may arise, they will read the documents and see that there are no grounds for concern.”

According to Ararat Mirzoyan, the Trump Route would also create new opportunities for both Russia and Iran.

“Through TRIPP, Iran, for example, will be able to gain access to the Black Sea. In effect, a new railway connection is being created from the Persian Gulf to the Black Sea.”

He also said that other countries had shown interest in the Trump Route initiative. Mirzoyan reminded journalists that it is an Armenian-American project. However, he noted that cooperation with third parties would be possible on separate components, including power transmission lines, pipelines and other infrastructure.

According to the minister, preliminary talks with partners from various countries are already under way, although he did not specify which countries were involved.

Preliminary plans already exist on rare minerals

According to Ararat Mirzoyan, cooperation with the United States in the field of critical minerals and rare earth elements represents a new direction in bilateral relations.

“Some rare metals are extremely important for the production of highly specialised goods such as chips and semiconductors. We are now essentially trying to connect the existing areas of cooperation with this new direction.”

He recalled that Armenia and the United States had already begun cooperation in the fields of artificial intelligence, semiconductors and energy.

The minister noted that there is growing global interest in rare mineral supply chains and said Armenia now has an opportunity to become one of the key hubs within these logistics routes.

Mirzoyan also said there are already preliminary outlines regarding investments in the sector and the types of minerals involved. He promised that “very concrete manifestations” of the agreements reached would emerge in the near future.

Endorsement of ruling party?

Armenia’s opposition and some analysts argued that the US secretary of state’s visit ahead of the country’s upcoming elections amounted to support for the ruling party and its leader, Nikol Pashinyan.

Their claims were reinforced by remarks Rubio made in Yerevan while addressing Armenian Foreign Minister Ararat Mirzoyan:

“You, the prime minister and the entire team are charting a path towards a brighter and more independent future for Armenia. And we are pleased to express our support for this vision, this courage, your dedication and willingness to work for the country’s future. We are proud to be part of all this, and we are ready to do more together.”

Responding to questions about whether the visit was intended as political backing, Mirzoyan told journalists that anyone who believed Rubio’s visit was needed to boost the ruling party’s ratings was “detached from reality”.

“Our ratings are sufficiently high. We have direct dialogue with the citizens of Armenia. And I can say even more: we see very strong and very clear public support for the peace agenda we are pursuing, for democratisation and for strengthening sovereignty,” he said.

Expert opinion

Political analyst Narek Minasyan commented in particular on the Charter on Comprehensive Strategic Partnership between Armenia and the United States. In his view, the document demonstrates that the partnership is “moving to a qualitatively new level”.

World.title: UK imposes sanctions on three companies registered in Georgia
World.content:
New UK sanctions against Russia

The UK has expanded its sanctions against Russia and added three Georgian companies to the list. The British government published a statement announcing the measures.

The statement says authorities targeted three Georgian companies that operate “Russia-oriented exchanges” and attempt to circumvent sanctions.

According to the document, the sanctions apply to Georgia-based companies Arvix LLC, Rapira Group LLC and Aifory LLC.

Under the sanctions, UK authorities will freeze all financial assets belonging to the three companies that fall under British jurisdiction. In addition, individuals and businesses operating in the UK face a complete ban on any economic, commercial or financial cooperation with the companies.

London said the new sanctions aim to restrict the activities of cryptocurrency and financial networks that help Russia circumvent international sanctions.

The UK government introduced a total of 18 new sanctions measures. The sanctions target companies based in Russia, the United Kingdom, Georgia, Kyrgyzstan, the United Arab Emirates, Panama and El Salvador.

What do we know about the sanctioned companies?

The Rapira Group LLC group appears most frequently in international analytical reports.

Blockchain analytics company Elliptic says Rapira registered in Georgia but also maintained an office in Moscow and worked extensively with the Russian cryptocurrency market.

According to reports, Rapira provided services converting roubles into cryptocurrency, enabling Russian companies and users to bypass international banking restrictions.

Elliptic says Rapira carried out direct transactions worth more than $72m with Grinex, a platform that Western authorities had previously linked to sanctions-evasion schemes.

International media outlets also reported that Russian law enforcement searched Rapira’s Moscow office in late 2025 in connection with alleged capital outflows.

The company registered on 9 November 2022. It is currently undergoing liquidation, with British citizen Ilya Akhaev listed as both owner and liquidator.

Aifory LLC, also registered in Georgia, appears in international reports under the name Aifory Pro. Reports say the company operated in Moscow, Dubai and Turkey.

According to Elliptic and other analytical platforms, Aifory offered users the ability to convert cash into cryptocurrency, as well as virtual cards linked to USDT, allowing access to Western online services restricted in Russia.

Reports also state that the platform took part in intermediary payment services between Russia and other countries, and that some transactions had links to Iranian cryptocurrency exchanges.

The company registered on 23 June 2023. According to business registry records, Mikhail Gevorkyan serves as both director and sole owner.

Information available publicly about Arvix LLC remains limited.

In the UK government document, authorities list the company among entities that helped Russia’s financial sector circumvent sanctions.

British authorities believe the company formed part of the same network that sought to weaken financial restrictions on Russia through cryptocurrency operations.

The company registered on 26 October 2023. According to business registry records, Tamaz Garaev is listed as both director and sole owner.

New UK sanctions against Russia

World.title: 108 years since Georgia adopted its Act of Independence as country marks occasion
World.content:
Georgia’s Independence Day 2026

On 26 May, Georgia celebrates Independence Day.

As the country marks the 108th anniversary of the adoption of the Act of Independence, heads of state, international organisations and diplomatic missions have sent congratulations to both the government and the Georgian people.

United States

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington remains firmly committed to Georgia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity within its internationally recognised borders.

Rubio said the United States supports the Georgian people in their pursuit of security, freedom and independence and stands ready to strengthen partnerships that serve “Georgia’s secure and prosperous future”.

Azerbaijan

President of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev described Georgia as a “friendly country and strategic partner”.

Aliyev highlighted the historical friendship, political dialogue and economic cooperation between the two countries. He also referred to his state visit to Georgia in April and said the sides had created favourable conditions for deeper regional cooperation.

Armenia

Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan described the deepening of relations with Georgia as one of Yerevan’s main foreign policy priorities.

Pashinyan stressed the importance of the strategic partnership format and regional cooperation.

Turkey

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan congratulated the Georgian people on Independence Day on behalf of “a friend and neighbour of Georgia”.

Erdoğan said the strategic partnership and cooperation between Tbilisi and Ankara serve the interests of regional stability and prosperity.

China

Chinese Premier Li Qiang said the strategic partnership between China and Georgia has “developed well” in recent years, particularly within the framework of the Belt and Road Initiative.

China’s president also sent a separate congratulatory message. Xi Jinping described Georgia as a “good friend and partner” and said Beijing is ready to take bilateral relations to “new heights”.

United Arab Emirates and Qatar

President of the United Arab Emirates Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan wished the Georgian government and people success, progress and prosperity.

Qatar’s Prime Minister Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani reaffirmed his commitment to strengthening close relations between the two countries and said Doha hopes to expand cooperation with Tbilisi.

European countries

King Philippe of Belgium congratulated the Georgian people and wished good health and success to President Mikheil Kavelashvili, who is backed by the ruling Georgian Dream party.

Croatian Prime Minister Andrej Plenković described 26 May as a symbol of the Georgian nation’s “unwavering strength and resilience”.

Bulgarian President Rumen Radev highlighted the historical and cultural ties between the two countries and stressed the importance of cooperation in the Black Sea region.

Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić and Prime Minister Đuro Macut referred to deepening relations between Tbilisi and Belgrade. Both leaders thanked Georgia for supporting Serbia’s territorial integrity.

Chairman of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina Denis Bećirović said friendly relations between the two countries would continue to strengthen.

Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko described Georgia’s Independence Day as “a symbol of strength and unity” for the Georgian people.

United Kingdom

King Charles III said he was proud of the “long-standing friendship” between the two countries and wished the Georgian people all the best in the coming year.

European Union and NATO

The EU delegation and embassies of member states said in a joint statement that the European Union continues to support Georgia’s independence, sovereignty and territorial integrity. The statement also stressed the importance of democratic reforms and European integration.

North Atlantic Treaty Organization’s public diplomacy office said the alliance remains firmly committed to Georgia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity and welcomed the Georgian people’s “freedom and resilience”.

Germany, Latvia and Poland

Germany’s embassy described 26 May 1918 as “a new chapter” in Georgia’s history and said Berlin continues to support a free and European Georgia.

German Ambassador Peter Fischer also said that Germany “stands alongside everyone who supports a free and European Georgia”.

Latvia’s Foreign Ministry said the country remains committed to supporting democracy in Georgia and its European aspirations.

Poland’s Foreign Ministry congratulated the Georgian people on Independence Day and extended its best wishes.

Israel

Israeli Ambassador to Georgia Hadas Meitzad described 26 May as a symbol of Georgia’s freedom and national pride. According to the ambassador, Georgia and Israel share historical ties, democratic principles and friendship.

The Pope

Pope Leo XIV wished the Georgian people peace and unity.

The Pope’s message placed particular emphasis on the importance of social solidarity, peacebuilding and charity.

Georgia’s Independence Day 2026

World.title: ‘For Georgia’ party to submit parliamentary resolution against annexation of Georgian territories
World.content:
Resolution against the annexation of Georgian territories

The For Georgia party plans to submit a draft resolution to Georgia’s parliament concerning an agreement signed on 9 May between Russia and the de facto authorities in Tskhinvali, as well as Moscow’s policy of annexation.

One of the party’s leaders, Shalva Kereselidze, said during a briefing that the so-called agreement on the “deepening of allied cooperation” represents another highly dangerous stage in the de facto annexation of the Tskhinvali region.

According to him, the document represents a step against Georgia’s sovereignty and statehood and envisages the full integration of various sectors of the occupied region into the Russian Federation.

Kereselidze also criticised the government’s position, saying the ruling Georgian Dream party has remained silent on the issue.

“Tomorrow is 26 May, Georgia’s Independence Day, and unfortunately we once again mark this symbolic date against the backdrop of the annexation of occupied territories and government silence,” he said.

According to Kereselidze, parliament currently remains “the only space” capable of giving a clear political and legal assessment of Russia’s policy.

The party of former Prime Minister Giorgi Gakharia is demanding a clearer response from the government. Kereselidze argues that the ruling team still has an opportunity to begin acting in defence of state interests.

The party is urging parliament to support a resolution against the annexation of Georgian territories. It is also calling on the government to “end its inaction”, restore active diplomatic efforts and strengthen cooperation with international partners to keep the issue of occupied territories on the international agenda.

Context

On 9 May 2026, Russian President Vladimir Putin and the leader of the self-proclaimed South Ossetia, Alan Gagloev, met at the Kremlin and signed a new agreement.

According to official explanations, the document aims to “deepen allied cooperation” between Russia and South Ossetia. However, the content of the agreement has reignited debate in the region over how close Moscow may be to annexing South Ossetia.

According to the text, the sides plan to harmonise legal norms, create conditions for the free movement of capital, goods and labour, and establish a common economic space. The agreement places particular emphasis on the gradual integration of energy, transport and telecommunications systems.

The Kremlin says it will continue participating in efforts to address socio-economic issues in Tskhinvali. The agreement also envisages deeper cooperation in social and cultural spheres, including labour rights and social protection.

Resolution against the annexation of Georgian territories

World.title: Azerbaijan marks Independence Day
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, May 28. Independence Day is celebrated in Azerbaijan today, on May 28.

The 20th century entered history not only as the century of science and technology, but also as the century of national revival, liberation of peoples from colonialism, and establishment of national states.

The revolution in Russia in 1917 put an end to the rule of the Romanov dynasty. Consequently, the Russian Empire disintegrated. The nations had to decide their own fate.

Therefore, the Azerbaijan Democratic Republic was proclaimed on May 28, 1918.

The Azerbaijan Democratic Republic became the first democratic republic not only in Azerbaijan, but also in the whole East.

It was a parliamentary republic. Its state attributes - flag, anthem, coat of arms - were adopted. The colors of the republic's flag reflected the formula "Turkism, Islamism, and modernity".

However, the Azerbaijan Democratic Republic existed for only 23 months. On April 28, 1920, Azerbaijan was occupied by the 11th Bolshevik Army, and the republic fell.

Previously, May 28 was celebrated as Republic Day in Azerbaijan. The state holiday has been celebrated as Independence Day since 2022.

World.title: Azerbaijan's SSS chief attends meeting of CIS Council of Heads of Security and Special Services Agencies
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, May 27. On May 26, Head of the State Security Service of the Republic of Azerbaijan, Colonel General Ali Naghiyev, took part in the 58th meeting of the Council of Heads of Security and Special Services Agencies of the member states of the Commonwealth of Independent States, held in Russia’s Irkutsk region, Trend reports citing the State Security Service.

Important decisions aimed at strengthening regional security were adopted during the meeting. Participants conducted a detailed analysis of the results of anti-terrorism measures implemented in previous years and identified specific future steps. In addition, the attendees agreed on new formats of cooperation for joint efforts against transnational terrorism and religious radicalism.

Paying special attention to the rapid development of technologies, members of the Council considered it appropriate to adopt a conceptual document containing recommendations on the use of artificial intelligence in the activities of the security agencies of CIS countries. It was emphasized that the implementation of this document would significantly enhance the scientific potential and operational capabilities of the relevant structures.

During the event, Colonel General Ali Naghiyev delivered a comprehensive report on the numerous threats to international stability and the security of transport and communication lines that have emerged recently, as well as on new manifestations of terrorism and the measures being carried out in Azerbaijan in this field. Stressing the serious impact of the complex geopolitical situation on the operational environment in the region, he highlighted the particular importance of information exchange and cooperation among partner agencies in countering threats to the security system, emphasizing the need to further strengthen joint efforts.

Within the framework of the meeting, participants held an extensive exchange of views on the future prospects and strategy of cooperation among the special services of CIS member states, as well as on the tasks ahead. Documents aimed at strengthening multilateral cooperation in the field of security were also signed.

World.title: Man avoids jail after indecently abusing woman he met on Tinder
World.content:
A man who indecently abused a woman he met on a dating app has avoided time behind bars.

Warning: This story includes descriptions of indecent sexual abuse.

Steven Murray, 36, matched with the woman on Tinder in February 2024, with the pair messaging on the platform before moving their conversation to Snapchat.

The ACT Supreme Court heard that while the conversation had become sexual in nature, the woman had told Murray, "I don't do sexual things on a first date."

The pair eventually met at a coffee shop before they went back to his home to watch a movie together.

They began consensually kissing, but then Murray began repeatedly indecently touching his victim's body, despite her telling him, "OK, stop now, that's enough" and pushing him away.

The court heard he said, "Wait, let me, just let me" at one stage while he was indecently touching her body as she was trying to push him away.

Murray then exposed his genitals to the woman, who froze and told him, "That's enough, stop."

The woman made up an excuse to leave, but Murray followed her to the front door, put his hand on her throat and pushed her against the wall where he began kissing her, despite the woman again telling him "that's enough".

He held the woman's hands above her head and continued to indecently touch her and said, "Just let me" before she pushed him away and left.

Woman 'eloquently explained' impact

Murray pleaded guilty to two counts of committing an act of indecency without consent and one count of committing an act of indecency in the third degree.

In sentencing, Justice Belinda Baker rejected a defence submission that the encounter was "complex, awkward and messy".

She found the woman had made her boundaries clear from the outset and had repeatedly communicated her lack of consent through both words and actions.

Justice Baker found Murray was "concerned only with his own sexual gratification" and persisted in the assault.

"The fact she consented to kissing and cuddling did not complicate the encounter," Justice Baker said.

"She made it clear … she did not consent to more sexualised contact.

"He did not apologise or respect her clear expression of consent."

Steven Murray was sentenced to 18 months' imprisonment to be served in the community under an intensive corrections order. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Justice Baker said the woman had "eloquently explained" the impact of the offending in her victim impact statement to the court.

The court heard the woman described how Murray's offending had turned her into "a shadow of the person she used to be".

She said Murray had chosen to ignore her when she used words telling him to stop.

"When you heard the words, 'no', 'stop' and 'that's enough' you chose to ignore them," she said.

"You said, 'Just wait' before you continued to violate me and … you broke me."

Justice Baker said the woman had wrongly blamed herself for the offence for about a year.

Murray was sentenced to 18 months' imprisonment to be served in the community under an intensive corrections order.

He was also ordered to undertake sexual offence-specific treatment and engage with mental health services.

World.title: Modelling suggests 'second wave' of algal bloom in Spencer Gulf
World.content:
Modelling predicts that the algal bloom that has plagued South Australia's coastlines since March 2025 will be moving further through the Spencer Gulf in the next few months.

The gulf, which is situated between the Yorke and Eyre peninsulas, had been thought to mostly escape the worst of the bloom, until early this year when it appeared in the previously untouched south-western tip of the Yorke Peninsula.

Since then, Karenia cristata has shown up more and more on the eastern coastline of the Spencer Gulf, concerning some communities and businesses.

However, other regional residents have stressed that people need to remain alert but not alarmed when it comes to the bloom.

The new modelling from oceanographer Jochen Kaempf is now predicting further growth in the gulf, with the harmful brevetoxin travelling northward, further into the gulf and hanging "around much longer".

The Spencer Gulf is located between the Eyre Peninsula on the west and the Yorke Peninsula on the east. (Supplied: Google Maps)

Dr Kaempf's modelling follows an announcement from the Department of Primary Industries SA (PIRSA) last week, confirming the presence of Karenia in Boston Bay and other parts of the lower Eyre Peninsula.

According to PIRSA's website, elevated levels of Karenia have been detected at seven of the 32 onshore testing sites on the Eyre Peninsula, with Boston Bay recording the most with 372,480 cells per litre.

Jochen Kaempf's modelling predicts the algal bloom will move through Spencer Gulf over the next few months. (Supplied: Jochen Kaempf)

New model predicts movement

In 2025, Dr Kaempf developed a modelling prediction showing the movement of the algal bloom, which indicated it would go up into Gulf St Vincent based on currents, nutrients and water temperature.

Jochen Kaempf says conditions are similar to last year. (ABC News: Brant Cumming)

Using algae numbers released by the South Australian Research and Development Institute [SARDI] last week and scientific data including current movements, Dr Kaempf has released a new model predicting its potential for growth into Spencer Gulf.

"In this model, it starts in May and uses the temperature and salinity and currents that exist as a starting point, and only adds algae at a concentration of 100 cells per millilitre," Dr Kaempf said.

"And in this simulation, this patch now spreads slowly along the west coast northward in the Spencer Gulf and reaches by about August, September, October the upper Spencer Gulf.

" The weird thing to me is we actually have similar conditions like we had last year. "

Dr Kaempf said he predicted the algal bloom would "hang around much longer" than was thought.

"Now we have the same situation; the algal bloom was actually declared over, but we are in a similar season.

"Last year, the algae bloom started in late March … now we have another hotspot around Boston Bay.

Jochen Kaempf says this is potentially the second wave of the algal bloom. (ABC News: Daniel Taylor)

" With my expertise, I can see that this is potentially the second wave, I call it. "

Citizen science helps get results

At North Shields beach, about 11 kilometres north of Port Lincoln, resident Wendy Lambert walks down the jetty every day and throws a bucket out, gathering samples of water to put through a homemade filter she has built to gather samples of water and to look for toxins.

Wendy Lambert collects and tests water samples near her home in North Shields. (ABC Eyre Peninsula: Emma Pedler)

Ms Lambert is one of an army of citizen scientists around the state who work alongside trained scientists within the Phytoplankton of South Australia group, in an ongoing, collective effort to track the movement of the harmful algal bloom in South Australian waters.

Earlier this week, Ms Lambert said she was contacted by friends walking on the beach who discovered just under 1,000 fish, some still gasping for air when the tide went out.

Wendy Lambert works with trained scientists to sample water for Karenia levels. (ABC Eyre Peninsula: Emma Pedler)

"There were all these tiny bait fish, sardines or something small scattered around," Ms Lambert said.

"They looked very healthy; they were shiny and bendy. That was a bit concerning, and before that I'd found Karenia in my water samples off the North Shields jetty and Louth Bay jetty."

Ms Lambert said she had seen fish washing up as early as April.

"Lots of pufferfish … there was a fairy penguin [and] a New Zealand octopus, which I'd never seen before," she said.

Wendy Lambert funds her citizen science research out of her own pocket. (ABC Eyre Peninsula: Emma Pedler)

Ms Lambert said government and citizen scientists were working together in a symbiotic "hunter-gather" style.

"They're the ones that need to know, and that's where the citizen science comes in … we can work hand in hand," she said.

"We can hunt it and if we find it, if they're interested, they can have another look."

Keeping perspective

District Council of the Lower Eyre Peninsula's acting chief executive Sacheen Hopewell said people should "be alert but not alarmed".

Sacheen Hopewell encourages locals to get their information from the experts. (ABC North and West SA: Jenae Madden)

"I think the speculation and the innuendo are almost as harmful to industry and the economy … and the confidence of our local community and industry as well," she said.

"We encourage everyone to get their data from the government experts, from PIRSA and SARDI.

"It's being actively managed, and I think as a council we're comfortable that those agencies are doing their job and keeping us informed."

Ms Hopewell said even though elevated levels had been detected, it was important to keep perspective with outbreaks in metro areas reaching counts into the millions — compared to the hundreds of thousands in the local region.

Multiple lines of evidence needed

A PIRSA spokesperson said while ongoing monitoring continued to rule out the presence of Karenia algae in the vast majority of South Australian waters, the state government has been clear that there was no guarantee it would not return.

"The government is aware of, and acknowledges, the modelling produced by Jochen Kaempf and others," they said.

Wendy Lambert found a New Zealand octopus washed up near North Shields. (Supplied: Wendy Lambert)

"However, the bloom has evolved differently to some modelled scenarios at various stages of the event, reinforcing the need to rely on multiple lines of evidence, including field sampling, satellite observations, and oceanographic monitoring to develop improved early detection and predictive capability."

The PIRSA spokesperson said water testing occurred twice weekly in areas of elevated Karenia activity, such as what was being experienced near the lower Eyre Peninsula.

"In addition to regular testing, the state government has also invested in six early detection and environmental monitoring buoys, including one in Boston Bay, which can provide early detection of harmful algal blooms."

World.title: Wettest May weather in decades as El Niño takes a rain check
World.content:
A series of low-pressure systems are drenching Australia this week, quickly turning this May into one of the wettest on record for parts of the country's east.

The focus today is north-east NSW and south-east Queensland where summer-like humidity and instability could bring intense downpours, along with gusty winds and hail.

A separate system is also bringing rain and storms to WA ahead of a more intense burst of gales, rain and storms set to sweep across southern states from Sunday to Tuesday.

Loading...

Summer-like storms for Qld and NSW

With the Pacific now on the brink of El Niño and parts of eastern Australia re-entering drought earlier this year, a wet May is critical for the nation's agricultural prospects.

But this month's rainfall has surpassed all expectations, culminating in four separate low-pressure systems in the space of just five days on Australia's weather charts.

The first low in the series has already soaked south-east states and produced some the heaviest rain in years, including:

86 millimetres in 48 hours at Dubbo, NSW — wettest May two-day spell on record

62mm in 24 hours at Balook, Vic — heaviest May rain in least 27 years

73mm in 24 hours at Gray, Tas — heaviest May rain in 9 years.

The low tracked south across Bass Strait on Wednesday and triggered further heavy rain on Tasmania's east coast with another 100mm plus falling at Gray by sunset.

While the first low is now tracking off Tasmania's south coast a second low is intensifying near the Queensland-NSW border.

Rain sweeps across Kangaroo Ground on Tuesday. (Supplied: Paula Linton)

This next low already triggered rain and storms on Tuesday afternoon from central Queensland to central NSW, with torrential falls of up to 40mm in an hour sweeping into Brisbane during the late afternoon.

Heavy rain along with thunderstorms will continue today with potentially severe storms across south-east Queensland and north-east NSW.

What stands out only days from winter is the high amounts of moisture, atmospheric instability and wind shear, three ingredients commonly found during major summer storm outbreaks.

As a result, thunderstorms could merge into organised bands and produce damaging wind gusts, large hail and intense downpours, particularly from about Newcastle to Bundaberg.

Thunderstorms aside, the low is also generating widespread rain with modelling predicting localised totals in excess of 50mm in just a few hours, triggering a Flood Watch for nine NSW catchments from Newcastle to the Orara river.

Up to 100mm will fall in NSW's north during the next 48 hours with well over 50mm possible in southern Queensland. (ABC News)

For Brisbane, the heaviest rain and greatest risk of severe weather is from about mid-morning to mid-afternoon.

Sydney lies just near the southern periphery of the low's influence and therefore has a less certain forecast and could see anything from heavy rain to a mostly dry day.

The low will then track into the Tasman on Friday but still drive rain onto the coast and ranges from about Sydney to Brisbane, boosting event totals to near 100mm in some parts.

WA rain relief ahead of weekend storm

While eastern Australia has seen multiple rain events this month, WA farmers have been forced to wait for a break.

Thankfully on Wednesday a cloudband arrived off the Indian Ocean, although rain yesterday was mostly confined to areas south of about Perth.

Solid falls then swept up the west coast and further inland overnight to the Central West, totalling well above 20mm in some regions.

However, a much more significant weather system is forecast to develop this weekend.

A low-pressure system approaching the west coast should rapidly deepen on Sunday, generating gales and widespread rain.

Loading...

Some modelling indicates the central pressure of the low could drop to near 980 hectopascals off the south-west capes, equivalent to the kind of pressure seen in category 2 tropical cyclones.

Under this scenario, wind gusts along the lower west coast of WA, including around Perth, could reach destructive speeds of 125 km/h which is strong enough to uproot trees and lead to power outages and slight structural damage.

Other models have a slightly less severe low, but regardless another band of rain and storms will arrive this weekend and falls near the west coast could again easily exceed 20mm.

Continued soaking for eastern states

A third low pressure system will cause showers and fresh winds to re-develop across south-east Australia this weekend, however far more impactful weather is likely when the WA system arrives.

The powerful low from WA, the fourth to directly impact southern Australia within a week, should sweep into the Bight on Monday and generate another round of showers and strong winds across south-east states into Tuesday.

It is too early to know whether or not wind damage will occur, however modelling is in solid agreement that agricultural parts of SA, most of Victoria and southern inland NSW will receive at least another 15mm of rain.

Rain is ahead for the whole of southern Australia during the next 8 days with falls for almost every agricultural region. (ABC News)

Remarkably, a fifth low could then bring another burst of showers, starting in WA on Tuesday and spreading to the east from midweek.

Surprise May soaking now wettest in decades

This May has already been the wettest in decades for parts of central and south-east Australia.

Some of the more noteworthy totals to 9am Wednesday include:

Renmark, SA 123mm — wettest May on record (data to 1889)

Walpeup, Vic 68mm — wettest May since 1992

Dubbo, NSW 134mm — wettest May since 1983

Urandangi, Qld 67mm — wettest May since 1968.

Despite the soaking this month, long range outlooks are still in firm agreement that El Niño and a drier than normal winter and spring are the most likely outcome later this year.

World.title: Brothers torn apart by Stolen Generations policies share their story
World.content:
It was a joyful moment when brothers Allen Edwards and Iain Seymour got to meet each other after 55 years apart.

Warning: This story contains images of an Indigenous person who has died.

But sad, too, with the realisation that a second generation of their family had been torn apart by Stolen Generations policies that disconnected both Mr Seymour and the mother he never met from their Aboriginal heritage.

"It's very emotional and, even now, it still affects me and I'm struggling to deal with it," Iain, 61, said.

"My legs went to jelly," Allen, 55, added.

"I didn’t know what to do, didn’t know what to say, but, no, it was a pretty good day in the end."

Brothers Iain Seymour and Allen Edwards at Colebrook Reconciliation Park, where they met in 2024. (ABC News: Lincoln Rothall)

Connections lead to meet-up

Iain and Allen's mother was Avis Gale (born Avis Edwards), who was taken from her mother in Koonibba, on South Australia's far west coast, at one week old in 1945.

She was instead brought up at Colebrook Home, in the southern Adelaide suburb of Eden Hills.

She became pregnant in 1964 and was whisked off to Melbourne, where she gave birth to Iain in January 1965.

He was adopted out to a white family that same year and Avis moved back to Adelaide, where she later had Allen and two daughters.

Avis Gale as a teenager, when she was known as Avis Edwards. (ABC News: Steve Opie)

After doubts about his genealogy, Iain did an online DNA test in 2023, found out he had Aboriginal heritage and then met with a service called Link Up SA that reunites Stolen Generations families.

The counsellor there, Sean Weetra-Newchurch, started by telling Iain it could take years to find his relatives — but was in for a surprise when he looked at Iain's birth certificate that named Avis Edwards as his mother.

"Within two seconds of looking at the paperwork, he went 'you've got your mum's eyes … I know your brother'," Iain recalled.

"So what was supposed to take three years or 10 years took about 30 seconds."

Water flows like tears at the Fountain of Tears in Colebrook Reconciliation Park. (ABC News: Steve Opie)

Allen and Mr Weetra-Newchurch's families had been close family friends for decades.

Allen and Iain met at the site of Colebrook Home — now Colebrook Reconciliation Park on Shepherds Hill Road — in February 2024.

Stolen Generations policies saw many Indigenous Australian children taken from their parents and raised without their culture, often in institutions like Colebrook Home.

"It was hard, you know. It was very hard in the home," Avis says in a voice recording activated when a button is pressed on a post in the park.

Mother prominent in advocacy

Colebrook Home was run in Adelaide by an evangelical Christian organisation called United Aborigines Mission from 1944 until the state government forced it to close in 1972.

"They were training the children to be white," Allen said.

Colebrook Home in 1969 from a segment on the ABC current affairs program This Day Tonight. (ABC)

Colebrook Reconciliation Park's roots began with the Blackwood Reconciliation Group (BRG), which formed as a study group in 1994.

A week after the Bringing Them Home report into the Stolen Generations came out in 1997, the BRG organised a rally at the site of Colebrook Home.

Among the about 2,000 people who turned out was Avis Gale.

She continued to be involved with the group until she died in 2020.

Avis Gale speaking at Colebrook Reconciliation Park in 1998. (ABC News)

Allen is also part of the group and Iain has also become involved more recently, as part of his journey to understand his Aboriginality.

"I was brought up as a white fella, but I've been learning about 58 years of missing heritage and missing culture," Iain said.

New meaning to sad words

Within the park there is a plaque naming Avis as one of the children who called Colebrook home, along with the prominent Indigenous advocate Lowitja O'Donoghue, who was also involved with the BRG.

There is also another plaque with a poem on it written by Avis:

"My baby, my baby, please give back my baby." A mother's words fall upon the deaf ears of authority. Hearts break, tears fall, fear cries out from wrenched hands and arms of a mother and child, separated. Feel the pain, touch the ache, caress the tears. Through ignorance and indifference came the disruption and destruction of family life.

Flowers left for Mother's Day at the Grieving Mother sculpture at Colebrook Reconciliation Park. (ABC News: Lincoln Rothall)

Before Allen knew of his brother Iain, or that his mother had had a baby that was taken, he assumed the poem was about his mother's own Stolen Generations story.

"By the looks of it, she told absolutely no-one, kept it to herself all these years," Allen said.

"I'll look at that plaque now in a different way every time I see that now."

Avis eventually got to know her mother — a Kokatha woman — and would return to Koonibba and Ceduna to connect with her heritage.

Education through personal stories

Colebrook Reconciliation Park is owned by the Aboriginal Lands Trust and maintained by the BRG.

The group runs about 100 educational tours at the park a year, mostly for school and university groups.

Allen Edwards and Iain Seymour discuss the Stolen Generations during educational tours. (ABC News: Lincoln Rothall)

An Indigenous person — often one connected with Colebrook — is on hand to share their personal story.

Both Allen and Iain are involved, like their mother before them.

"Now that she's passed, I feel even more committed to building on the site here," Allen said.

"It has a renewed meaning for me, I think, knowing Mum was here all of those years and for us to be able to tell her story at this place."

The Blackwood Reconciliation Group has met in the southern Adelaide suburb for more than 30 years. (ABC News: Steve Opie)

While the Stolen Generations policies that led to so many Indigenous children being removed from their parents ended more than 50 years ago, Allen said his and Iain's story showed they still had an effect today.

"It's an intergenerational trauma," he said.

"So Mum was first generation Stolen Generation, I’m second generation Stolen Generation, my children are third generation and the reason they say that is when I hear stories of my mum in the home, that affects me and I feel that.

"My children are starting to learn the stories of their grandmother in the home and that affects them and they’ll tell their children."

Reconciliation process continuing

Mike Lawson was among the earliest members of the BRG.

He said it was important that Indigenous people like Avis and now Allen and Iain were involved.

They often chat while sitting around a fire circle in the park.

Mike Lawson recalls becoming friends with former Colebrook Home children. (ABC News: Lincoln Rothall)

"We could be sitting down with Avis or we could be sitting down with Lowitja O'Donoghue or Doris Kartinyeri or Mona Olsson," Mr Lawson said.

"They were people who were telling us what it was like to be a child taken from their parents — maybe not seeing their parents for many, many years until they became adults.

"That made a big difference to my education and informed me about Aboriginal affairs in ways that I have never been informed in the past … because Aboriginal people are still living a different life to many of us and have challenges that they must meet.

"We sometimes don't understand those — but we can understand them if we talk to people like Allen and Iain."

The BRG holds a march during National Reconciliation Week each year, ending at Colebrook Reconciliation Park.

This year the Blackwood Reconciliation Walk is being held on Sunday, May 31.

A documentary has been made about the brothers' story, called Iain and Allen: Full Circle.

World.title: Teenager stabbed during fight at Melbourne shopping centre
World.content:
A teenager has been stabbed during a fight at a shopping centre in Melbourne's west.

Police were called to Highpoint Shopping Centre on Rosamond Road in Maribyrnong just after 7pm on Wednesday.

Investigators were told there had been a fight between a group of youths near the cinema and dining outlets.

A teenage boy was found with a laceration to his lower back.

He was taken to hospital with non-life-threatening injuries.

The stabbing happened during the dinnertime rush. (ABC News)

The rest of the group fled before police arrival.

Shoppers and diners could be seen gathering outside the doors to the shopping centre as more police arrived.

No-one has been arrested at this stage.

Police are appealing for anyone with information or footage to contact Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000 or online.

World.title: Bike shop burns down, factory torched on fiery night in Melbourne
World.content:
Witnesses have described hearing explosions coming from inside a Brunswick bike shop as a fire destroyed the business in Melbourne's inner north last night.

Emergency services were called to the Prentice Street shop at about 9:15pm after smoke began billowing from under the doorway of the building.

Police said no-one was inside at the time and the cause of the fire remained under investigation.

Witnesses noticed smoke billowing from the Brunswick bike store. (ABC News)

Volunteers from The Big Umbrella Foundation, a street meals service, were inside a neighbouring property at the time.

Lucy said they were packing up for the night when they heard what they thought was a car alarm going off.

She said some members of the team went to investigate and saw the fire.

"In a matter of five minutes the whole place was up in flames," Lucy said.

" We could hear actual explosions going off in there. "

Thick smoke blanketed Brunswick as firefighters battled the bike store fire. (ABC News)

The emergency food service was forced to evacuate its premises.

Thick plumes of smoke were seen coming from the building as firefighters attacked the blaze from above.

A police spokesperson said a crime scene had been established.

Flames tore through the roof of the Brunswick bike store. (ABC News)

Arson attack in Keysborough

Meanwhile, police are investigating a separate early morning blaze in a row of adjoining factories in Keysborough, in Melbourne's south-east.

Police said an offenders broke into a vehicle accessories business on Olive Grove about 12:15am.

"A fire was started before offenders fled the scene," a Victoria Police spokesperson said.

Police say offenders broke into the Keysborough vehicle accessories factory and set it alight. (ABC News)

Firefighters contained the blaze to the one premises.

Authorities said no-one was inside the building at the time.

"It is yet to be determined if this incident is linked to any others," police said.

Anyone who witnessed the incident, has footage or information is urged to contact Crime Stoppers on 800 333 000 or online.

World.title: Load limits on Victorian bridges 'wreaking havoc' on agricultural industry
World.content:
When the load limit of a bridge in regional Victoria was lowered to 45 tonnes, B-double trucks heading to a nearby hay processing facility had to add about 80 kilometres to their round trip.

The change to the 84-year-old Avoca-Bealiba Road bridge in the Pyrenees Shire effectively banned most heavy agricultural and freight vehicles from using it.

Pyrenees Hay is located about 10km away from the bridge, and manager Julie Bartlett said every extra kilometre trucks had to travel affected her business and the local agricultural industry.

"For us it's a financial cost, because our trucks have to travel an extra 30 or 40km to get here and also that distance back," Ms Bartlett said.

"It's a huge cost to us because they can't use [the bridge] if they're over 45 tonnes.

"Ninety per cent of our trucks that come in here are B-doubles, which are not allowed to use that road.

" It's wreaking havoc on the whole agricultural industry in this area — everyone uses this road, it's quite a big agricultural area and there's a lot of transport movements through this area with grain, stock, hay. "

Bridge Five on Avoca-Bealiba road in Natte Yallock had its load limited to 45 tonnes a year ago. (Supplied: Greater Ballarat Alliance of Councils)

Every kilometre counts

Howell Livestock Transport's Graham Howell is another truck driver who cannot use the Avoca-Bealiba Road due to the lower bridge limit, adding 12km to every trip he takes through the region.

Mr Howell said that during a time when fuel costs are sky high, every kilometre counts.

"Sometimes we can pass the cost on, but then it goes to the farmers or whoever we’re working for and if we can't pass the cost on, it has to be absorbed by our business," he said.

"Every time there is a load limit on a road it makes a huge difference.

"The whole road network [is] going backwards and has been for the last few years, especially now as the trucks are getting bigger."

Graham Howell says load limits popping up on bridges are costing his business. (Supplied: Greater Ballarat Alliance of Councils)

Pyrenees Shire mayor Damian Ferrari estimated it would cost his council $4 million to restore the Avoca-Bealiba bridge to a full-load capacity.

"The repair and replacement of bridges is extremely expensive, and the Pyrenees Shire, along with most rural shires, simply don't have the funding," Cr Ferrari said.

He said there were multiple bridges across his shire's road network with load limits.

"Our farmers rely on the road network to get their products from a farm gate to market," Cr Ferrari said.

"In recent years, the technical advancement with trucks has led to increased weights, and these bridges that were made many years ago simply don't cater for those new weights and heavy vehicles."

Regions fed up

Regional Victorian councils are facing growing financial pressure and struggling to maintain their existing deteriorating road and bridge networks.

As a result, some councils have lowered load limits and speed limits to prolong road infrastructure.

In the state's east, residents frustrated by the lowering of speed limits on country roads have taken to vandalising street signs.

In this financial year, while the state government had a target to fund the repair of 22 bridges in regional Victoria, its projections indicate it will only repair 20.

The Greater Ballarat Alliance of Councils says councils need more funding for regional roads. (Supplied: Greater Ballarat Alliance of Councils)

And the bridge issue is expected to worsen, with the Victorian government slashing its regional bridge repair target to seven in the 2026-2027 financial year.

Ahead of the Victorian election, the Greater Alliance of Ballarat Councils is calling on the Victorian government to reinstate a long-term country roads and bridges program for regional Victoria.

Each of the six councils within the alliance — Central Goldfields, Ballarat, Golden Plains, Hepburn, Moorabool and Pyrenees — said the anticipated cost of sealing and maintaining roads is higher than its income.

Alliance chair and City of Ballarat mayor Tracey Hargreaves said a different funding model was needed.

"Councils are being asked to do more with less all the time," Cr Hargreaves said.

"However, costs keep rising and funding has not been keeping pace.

"Local governments are responsible for large amounts of infrastructure but we rely on a really limited ratepayer base."

Councils doing their best

For Mr Howell, every load limit on a bridge is a loss in productivity, but he said councils were doing their best with what little they had.

"The shires are basically only getting their money from the ratepayers, so it's very difficult," he said.

"I'd hate to be in their position to try and squeeze the lemon.

"You can see [a regional-metro divide] with tunnels in Melbourne that most of us don't use, compared to the local roads we run up and down all the time every day.

"There's a huge difference, when you leave the city and start heading out. Every kilometre you go, you start to see [the roads] deteriorating."

The Victorian government said it had delivered a high number of bridge-strengthening projects across regional Victoria in the past year to support farmers and freight operators.

"Since we have delivered a high number of bridge-strengthening projects, we will now focus on the ongoing maintenance of our bridges and other planned upgrades," a spokesperson said.

World.title: As the debate heats up, migrants are quietly keeping the bush running
World.content:
In a sunny corner of an aged care facility in south-west NSW, registered nurse Vanessa Joy Hipolito is deep in conversation with resident Trisha Newton.

Moments like this that stay with her long after her shift at Allawah Lodge in Coolamon, a small town north of Wagga Wagga, is over.

"Our work can be really challenging, but it is also rewarding," Ms Hipolito said.

" It becomes even more meaningful when the families and the residents reach out and appreciate us. "

She is one of 14 migrant workers from the Philippines sponsored by the Coolamon Shire Council to work at the facility.

Council general manager Tony Donoghue said migrants had been filling a gap local workers could not.

"Prior to us going through that process, we had to restrict bed numbers," he said.

"Since we've brought this workforce over, it's a weight off our shoulders … [it] means we're able to offer more opportunities for our elderly to age in place."

Tony Donoghue says Filipino workers are essential to the running of Allawah Lodge. (ABC News: Emily Doak)

Over the last year, Australia's immigration intake and migration policies have become a topic of national discussion dominating this month's Farrer by-election and the federal budget.

The federal government has forecast net migration of 295,000 people this financial year — well down on the more than 530,000 migrants in 2022-23.

Meanwhile, Opposition Leader Angus Taylor has indicated that if the Liberal-National Coalition comes to power in 2028 it will cap immigration numbers based on the number of homes constructed each year.

"Never again will a government be able to bring in more people than our housing can support," Mr Taylor told parliament during his budget reply speech.

" We must allow the housing market to keep up. The Coalition will deliver one of the biggest cuts to immigration in Australian history. "

Mr Donoghue acknowledged housing is essential — the council spent $500,000 in 2023 building accommodation for its aged care workforce.

But he believes sweeping national migration policy changes could have serious ramifications for communities such as Coolamon.

"Encouraging people to come out and live regionally, work regionally, allows our regions to grow and is a really important part of how Australia develops."

University of Sydney postdoctoral research associate Sasha Block has recently been involved in a study looking at the role of migrants in Australia's healthcare workforce.

She said international workers constitute about 50 per cent of Australia's healthcare workforce, and in some regional communities the figures are higher.

"They bring quality care, a continuity of care. They also bring their culture, families… [an] enormous attitude to contribute," she said.

"But apart from that, it makes places vibrant … they contribute to the livability of regional places."

Sasha Block says research shows migrants can provide economic and social benefits to regional communities. (Supplied: Dr Sasha Block)

Migration critical to horticulture, agriculture

In one of Australia's largest citrus growing regions in South Australia's Riverland, second-generation farmer Phillip Kroehn runs a large-scale orange, mandarin and lemon operation.

He said without migrant workers, predominantly Pacific Australia Labour Mobility (PALM) scheme seasonal workers from the Pacific Islands, he would not be able to run his farm or have his fruit picked in time.

There are currently more than 32,000 overseas workers employed under the PALM scheme.

"The pickers I've got are here to do a job … and they're not taking anyone's housing," he said.

"They live in accommodation for about eight or nine months a year … and if it wasn't for them, I'm quite sure we'd still have fruit on the trees.

" It's not just the citrus industry. A lot of agriculture relies on immigration and people coming in to help us do our job. "

Citrus grower Phil Kroehn says migrant workers play a vital role on his South Australian farm. (ABC News: Anita Ward )

Back in New South Wales, Gundagai Meat Processors chief executive Will Barton agrees with wholeheartedly.

He too accommodates the 140 migrant workers he employs.

"The pressures that exist in the bush are very different to the pressures that exist in cities," Mr Barton said.

"[Don't] lump us in with everybody … recognise that there are unique challenges in the bush, which we've gone a long way to mitigating."

A recent survey by Citrus Australia shows 49 per cent of citrus farms have employed PALM workers, while the Australian Meat Processor Corporation said its research suggested up to 50 per cent of workers in the red meat processing sector are visa holders.

Mr Barton said current visa settings provide migrant workers with the opportunity to "try before they buy", as opposed to previous set-ups that focused on either highly skilled workers or backpackers on six month contracts.

Will Barton says his company provides accommodation to migrant workers. (ABC News: Emily Doak)

Benefits for economies, communities and migrants

Dr Block said a regional lens must be applied to Australia's migration policies, with place-based programs to help in their implementation.

"We really need to work with the specific place and their conditions and capabilities to make migration work for economies, communities and migrants," he said.

PALM scheme workers play an important role in many industries based in regional Australia. (Supplied: Peter Mares)

For Ms Hipolito that delicate balance has been achieved in Coolamon.

"I'm a single mother, so I'm doing this for my family," she said.

"Moving here makes me miss my family, but Coolamon is warm and very welcoming.

'It's really worthwhile … being here in Australia with great opportunities … I really hope they'll be more open to immigrants."

World.title: Australia news LIVE: Royal commission exposes gun registry intelligence gap, warning AUKUS has become Defence ‘centre of gravity’, Five divers found alive in Laos cave
World.content:
Bangkok: Five villagers who became trapped in a flooded cave in central Laos more than a week ago have been found alive by divers who discovered them sitting on a rock in the darkness, but two others are still missing.

The seven villagers entered the cave in Xaisomboun province on May 19, but heavy rain triggered flash flooding that blocked the exit, according to Lao and Thai rescue teams involved in the operation.

Rescuers work to reach seven people trapped in a cave in Xaisomboun province, Laos. Metta Tham Rescue Kalasin via AP

Thai rescuer Chakkit Taengtang posted video of himself in the cave saying divers were delivering food and water to the five and planning to extract them as soon as possible.

All of the villagers are men, according to a Facebook post by the Lao group Rescue Volunteer for People.

World.title: ASX set to slide, Wall Street hangs near its records as oil prices ease
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to slide, Wall Street hangs near its records as oil prices ease Stan Choe Updated May 28, 2026 — 6:36am ,first published 5:18am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

US stocks inched to more records after oil prices fell and eased the pressure on households and businesses worldwide. The S&P 500 edged up by less than 0.1 per cent and added to its all-time high set the day before. The Dow Jones Industrial Average climbed 182 points, or 0.4 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite gained 0.1 per cent as both indexes also set records. Wall Street has been boosted by US companies reporting surprisingly strong profits for the start of 2026, and the forecast is for them to continue. AP The Australian sharemarket is set to decline, with futures at 6.23am AEST pointing to a fall of 44 points, or 0.5 per cent, at the open. The ASX added 0.7 per cent on Wednesday. The Australian dollar was trading at US71.42¢. Stocks of companies with big fuel bills helped lead the way on hopes that lower oil prices will remove a big drag on their profits. Norwegian Cruise Line Holdings climbed 6.1 per cent, and United Airlines rallied 6.3 per cent. Delta Air Lines rose 3 per cent and set an all-time high.



Related Article Opinion

AI ‘Idolatry of profit’: Pope Leo takes on AI’s wannabe trillionaires Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil fell 4.6 per cent to $US92.25 after the ceasefire between the United States and Iran appeared to hold despite the US military launching what it called “self-defence” strikes in southern Iran. A barrel of benchmark US crude fell even more, 5.5 per cent, to settle at $US88.68 and is back to where it was in mid-April on hopes that the United States and Iran can reach an agreement to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and allow oil tankers to exit the Persian Gulf for deliveries again. Stocks have been able to run to records despite the painful inflation and uncertainty caused by high oil prices largely because companies have reported surprisingly strong profits for the start of 2026, and the forecast is for them to continue. Bath & Body Works rallied 9.7 per cent, and Abercrombie & Fitch climbed 8.9 per cent after both reported bigger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. That’s even as US consumers continue to say they’re feeling discouraged about the economy and inflation. Lululemon Athletica rose 2.9 per cent after reaching a deal with its founder, Chip Wilson, where it will add a former chief marketing officer of ESPN and a former co-CEO of On to its board of directors.



On the losing side of Wall Street was Dick’s Sporting Goods, which dropped 6 per cent despite delivering a profit for the latest quarter that edged past expectations. Analysts pointed to how much profit it wrung out of each dollar in revenue, which some called a bit weak. Oil-and-gas stocks also sank, hurt by the dropping prices for crude. Exxon Mobil fell 1.3 per cent, and Chevron slipped 1.3 per cent. Halliburton dropped 3.6 per cent to bring its gain for the year so far back toward 40 per cent. All told, the S&P 500 rose 1.24 to 7,520.36. The Dow Jones Industrial Average climbed 182.60 points to 50,644.28, and the Nasdaq composite gained 18.55 to 26,674.73. In the bond market, Treasury yields eased after falling oil prices took pressure off inflation. The yield on the 10-year Treasury slipped to 4.48 per cent from 4.50 per cent late Tuesday and from 4.67 per cent roughly a week ago. It’s a respite following recent gains for yields in bond markets worldwide, which threatened to slow economies and undercut prices for stocks and all kinds of other investments. High yields have already forced the average long-term US mortgage rate to its most expensive level since last summer, and they could curtail companies’ borrowing to build the artificial-intelligence data centres that have supported the US economy’s growth recently.



Related Article Opinion

Gina Rinehart The Rinehart-backed deal that’s created a smorgasbord for conspiracy theorists Elizabeth Knight Business columnist In stock markets abroad, indexes were mixed across Europe and Asia. South Korea’s Kospi was one of the world’s best performers and jumped 2.3 per cent after SK Hynix, which is a big beneficiary of the AI boom, soared 9.3 per cent. A day before, Micron Technology surged to become the latest Big Tech company to be worth more than $US1 trillion ($1.4 trillion) because of AI excitement. Its stock has more than tripled already in 2026, and analysts at UBS said Tuesday it could soar even more because of how fundamentally AI has improved demand for computer memory. It rose another 3.6 per cent Wednesday. AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.
