By treating the speaking animals so credulously, de Tores’ narrative device proves both humorous and affecting: Selkirk needs the conversation; Sleek, his regular feeding of goat livers. Eventually, we learn Selkirk has wronged his lover Effie terribly. Here, de Tores has some fun with the “kirk” pun, a Scottish term connoting the church and its judgement. Fuelled by a sense of shame and the (imagined) public gaze, Selkirk wonders if he hasn’t died at sea and awoken in a watery hell, consigned to deal alone with his shames, guilts, regrets and recriminations. He starts to miss his brothers. He strikes up conversation with a goat skull. Who wouldn’t? De Tores interrogates Selkirk’s character by having him confront a simple question: how does one inclined not to listen learn to do so? “[S]uffering is not a currency with which you can purchase absolution”, Sleek counsels. Seeking an accounting anyway, his animal brethren point out that anything truly unforgivable requires being unable to ask for forgiveness.



Existential questions nag at him: is he blessed to survive, or damned to? Is he better or worse off than some of the shipmates he once knew, sunk thousands of feet below the water’s surface, ignorant of hunger or worry or hope? By having Selkirk importune an imagined audience, de Tores does not suggest that Selkirk loses his sense of loneliness so much as he “forget[s] to be lonely” – a psychologically confronting state for a man so used to ignoring his circumstances. Having already changed from ne’er-do-well to accomplished navigator, forced to meet the island on its own terms, Selkirk is reasonably sanguine about being cast away: what scares him more is the thought of being “lost to all knowing”, a dying “more complete than any other.” Alexander Selkirk, the inspiration for Robinson Crusoe and the subject of Francesca de Tores’ novel, seen in a 1719 engraving on one of the Juan Fernandez Islands. Getty Images Editor's pick Literature prizes Randa Abdel-Fattah among authors on longlist for $60,000 Miles Franklin Literary Award De Tores convincingly recreates the language and interiority of the period, though she does allow for a few contemporary flourishes (“I swim and I swim until the only thought I have room for is breathe, breathe, breathe”). Expertly combining pathos, elegance, and paciness, drawing the reader in with gallows humour, by the time the trap door of de Torres’ novel swings open its brilliance seems undeniable. As Selkirk reflects, “I am furious when I eat, and desolate even when I frig myself, and in every way I know for certain that this island has ruined me. And yet I live”. Cast Away by Francesca de Tores is published by Bloomsbury ($33).

World.title: College of GPs says patient portals taken on 'good faith'
World.content:
Photo: supplied

Assurances that portals managing patient information were safe were not enough, says the president and chair of the Royal New Zealand College of General Practitioners (RNZCGP).

General practitioners are asking for the Ministry of Health to implement a vetting process for patient portals, after results of the Manage my Health inquiry.

The Privacy Commissioners found Health NZ and Manage My Health "failed in their responsibilities" to have adequate security controls when thousands of medical files were stolen in a cyber attack.

The review found Health NZ should have taken more steps to make sure that it was safe to pass on the information to patients through Manage My Health.

RNZCGP president Luke Bradford told Morning Report that since the Manage my Health breach, the college had realised it needs centralised standards.

"We took it on good faith and from the contracts we were given that the patient information will be protected adequately."

"It's now shown, obviously with this breach, that there are weaknesses."

The college is calling for a set of standards and certification GPs can we can look to.

Bradford said 60 to 70 percent of GP practices use patient portals like Manage My Health.

He said GPs themselves don't have the ability to properly test and probe the portals to be assured they are safe.

He said the portals are a useful tool for patients, allowing them to book appointments, request medication, see results, and have secure messaging with their doctor.

World.title: Calls for government funding to support marae
World.content:
Photo: RNZ / Dan Cook

Marae are calling for targeted funding to help them serve their communities and organise better emergency responses, as the government prepares to unveil its Budget for 2026.

Valerie Teraitua is the marae manager at Papatuānuku Kōkiri Marae in South Auckland's Māngere.

The marae has a number of services, including a māra kai, or community garden, a composting factory, a "pay-as-you-can" café and free fish on Wednesdays and Fridays.

Teraitua told RNZ the marae received support from philanthropic organisations, local government and corporate sponsors to deliver their services.

"We haven't really had any government funding as such because we are destined to have our own mana motuhake. But we know of other organisations that do amazing mahi and I think that, just one marae doing that is not enough."

Teraitua said marae were often the first places people go to in an emergency and should be resourced properly to deal with them.

"We have a value system of the way that we look after people.

"We're in positions to not only offer a service of manaakitanga, but everything's all in that one place. You've got your kitchen; you've got places where you can house people. My wish would be that marae be resourced because they take care of a holistic approach to the wellbeing of our people," she said.

She said that manaakitanga was not extended exclusively to Māori and the marae's popular Kai Ika programme - where the marae distributes unwanted or leftover fish heads and frames for free - attracts people from all over Auckland.

"The project distributes one tonne of fish at Māngere Centre Park every Wednesday and Friday from 10.30 till finish… it is the longest and the biggest drive through than any other fast-food outlet.

"I tell you, the diversity of the whānau that come from even out of Favona, some are coming from Mount Russell, some are coming from North Shore, these are whānau that are in need and they've just heard the good news that this project is available … it's a circular economy of not just food rescue, it's bringing people in and giving them a purpose to serve." she said.

RNZ spoke to Te Puu Ao trustee Auriole Ruka in the aftermath of Cyclone Vaianu, who organised temporary accommodation, food and clothing for Whangārei's homeless community at Terenga Paraoa marae.

Speaking to RNZ before the Budget, Ruka said she also relied on local community and council groups for support, rather than direct support from the government.

"Marae are already resourcing, in many ways, without pūtea (funds) the communities that are often not thought about when we're having these emergency responses.

"I think that's important because they provide manaaki and they've done that for generations, so pūtea isn't the main question that comes in when we're responding to that … it's more about what's our role and responsibility as mana whenua," she said

Ruka said her trust has a "small amount of dollars" in the bank, but the most important currency was the relationships and networks they had across region.

"They start to bring in kai, they start to bring in clothes, and even the small businesses that are around our marae start to kick in."

"They do it because of their currency of aroha."

Ruka said the ultimate goal is for marae completely self-sufficient, the cost of standing up an emergency response were often upfront and costly.

"What I would say in terms of the budget, not necessarily about pūtea, because there's been investments nationally, but if I look at it locally, regionally, and for iwi and hapū, it's acknowledging the place of marae in the whole response.

"It's funding up front marae responses, so that people who have to go back to work and prepare for the next wānanga don't have to be following through and trying to get reimbursements at such a low level that you wonder why it's even worth it.

"We'd have up front capital funding that's done in a trusting relationship, and the emergency management system would also think about the ongoing maintenance of these manaaki hubs and the equipment that's required," Ruka said.

The full details of Budget 2026 will be released on Thursday afternoon.

World.title: Reserve Bank governor expects OCR to go up to 'neutral level'
World.content:
Photo: RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

The governor of the Reserve Bank is expecting the official cash rate to go up to 3 or 3.25 percent in the future.

It has held the official cash rate unchanged at 2.25 percent, but only after the governor used her casting vote to break a deadlock.

The bank's monetary committee was split three-three between staying unchanged and raising to 2.5 percent.

Anna Breman told Morning Report the committee is expecting to hike the official cash rate at upcoming meetings.

She said it will go up to what is called the neutral level - neither speeding up nor slowing down the economy.

"If we don't hike were likely to get more persistent more enduring inflation and we want to avoid that."

She said they also wanted to avoid unnecessary volatility and economic output and therefore had to weigh the risk of inflation getting higher against weaker economic growth.

Breman acknowledged that some firms would pass the cost on to households.

"To prevent that from getting out of hand, we do think we need to tighten monetary policy a little bit when that means rate hikes."

She said while there was a main forecast, or central projections, there were also different scenarios.

"Because if the economy is weaker than we expect, and we see less inflation than we expect, well, then the OCR could be on hold over the coming meetings."

"But we could also see considerably higher inflation, and inflation becoming more embedded in the economy. And then we would actually have to do more rate hikes."

Breman said the goal was to ensure that inflation returns to the 2 percent target over the medium term.

She also said the 'indirect effects' of the Middle East crisis, like increased transport costs, would also contribute to any OCR hikes.

"And when we start seeing those kind of effects, that can get out of control. So we expect to see some of that and need to hike to push back on that.

"But we're also very clear that if we see that firms can take some of those costs in their profit margins, we would actually need to do less OCR hikes."

World.title: Raising a left-handed child in a right-handed world
World.content: Throughout history, left-handers have faced bias and been forced to convert to being right-handed for a range of reasons. These include cultural and religious ideas, with the left hand being associated with bad luck, and in some religions the use of the left hand considered a taboo.

World.title: Scientists not holding out hope for big Budget boost after year of cuts and sector overhaul
World.content:
Photo: RNZ / Mark Papalii

Scientists are adamant investing in the sector now will pay dividends later - but are not holding out much hope for a big Budget funding boost after a year of redundancies and funding cuts amid a major overhaul of the sector.

Last year saw the biggest shake-up to the science system in 30 years.

It saw Crown Research Institutes merge into Public Research Organisations, the scrapping of Callaghan Innovation, and a raft of new intiatives including: the establishment of the Gene Technology Regulator, an office to attract foreign investment, and an advisory council to the prime minister.

Budget 2025 cannibalised research and innovation funds to help fund the changes.

Minister of Science, Innovation and Technology Penny Simmonds would not comment on Thursday's Budget, but said researchers make an "extraordinary contribution" and the sector's significant reforms would create a more stable, strategic, and sustainable system.

Innovate or 'death spiral' - researcher

Lincoln Agritech chief executive Travis Glare said the sector's recent upheaval needed to be followed by stability and long-term vision.

"There's been real cuts to the science system over the last few years, which means the system struggles as you're basically losing people. You've got amalgamated science organisations - that takes a lot of money to merge organisations - and that's all money that's not going into actually doing the science."

Photo: Supplied / Lincoln Agritech

He hoped Budget 2026 would redirect money into research and development [R&D] - his company's core purpose - and 'blue-skies' or curiosity-driven research to enable a "discovery pipeline".

Glare said investing in science over more tangible public services could be a difficult argument for taxpayers, but he said long-term economic success hinged on innovation - and that required years of work.

"We're not actually building an economy that will pay for better healthcare and better education. The government is having to divide a much smaller pie every year and innovation is the only way we're getting out of this death spiral."

Glare said after years of what felt like "ad hoc" funding - a strategy for the sector was a brightspot.

"Not everyone is going to agree with it, but at least reseachers understand what the government is looking for."

In its report to the prime minister earlier this year, the Science and Technology Advisory Council outlined a framework for the government to signal investment priorities. It was based on four 'pillars' covering primary industries, environmental sustainability, technology, and health.

It said the country's poor economic performance reflected "deep-seated structural and external challenges" and targeted public investment in science, innovation, and technology [SI&T] offered "one of the most direct and high-impact pathways to restore momentum".

"This is reinforced by overwhelming international evidence that SI&T are core to lifting productivity, export competitiveness and economic growth.

"The country's scientists, researchers and entrepreneurs deliver strong results within the system's constraints, but barriers continue to limit their impact."

It urged the government to scale up investment once the framework proved its capability.

Photo: Waikato University

Co-president of the New Zealand Association of Scientists Troy Baisden said business R&D had flatlined recently, indicating the public system was not adequately supporting private investment and believed New Zealand did not appreciate the link between science R&D and productivity.

"There's a lack of a sense that much of our agricultural productivity came from investments 20-30 years ago in science."

He said small gains in the sector over the past year had been overshadowed by bigger losses and hoped the overhaul in the sector created a system that politicians could confidently invest in.

But optimism for this Budget was tempered.

"What we're really looking for at this point are no more cuts."

'Everything you touch came through ... research'

MacDiarmid Institute director Nicola Gaston said she was not expecting much in the Budget, but after a year characterised by disruption a commitment to boost funding - down the line - would be welcome.

Photo: Victoria University

"In the absense of new money this year, a plan to grow investment over time and ... more information about the process of funding so that it has a level of visibility to researchers [would be good].

"That level of uncertainty I think has created some level of distrust of the process, so I'd like to see more detail and something that looks like an actual plan."

Gaston said research funding, or "baseline funding for universities" was essential if the country wanted a workforce capable of navigating a "rapidly changing world".

"You need to have a functional research-informed education system, that means you need to fund research."

Auckland University associate professor of sociology Sereana Naepi agreed, maintaining there would be no Rocket Lab without a healthy education and undergraduate research pipeline.

Photo: Supplied

But she acknowledged investing in such a system could be a hard sell for the public given a lot of the work was unseen.

"But everything you touch came through the research space at some point and so while we're not an immediate day-to-day thing in a lot of people's minds, if you like your phone, if you like your computer, if you like immunisations or if you like that ability to put a stent in your heart - it usually came out of the research sector before it got privatised."

Long-term direction promised

Science Minister Penny Simmonds - the third to hold the portfolio this government term - said the science reforms were focussed on getting the settings right so public investment "delivers stronger impact, with clearer priorities and better connections to industry".

She said R&D continued to be supported through public investment and tools like the R&D Tax Incentive.

"Which is helping lift business investment in innovation, which is extremely important as two-thirds of the R&D that happens in New Zealand takes place in private businesses.

"The upcoming Science Investment Plan will set out the government's long-term direction for science, innovation and technology and will provide greater certainty for the sector."

She said she was unable to comment on what may or may not be included in the Budget ahead of Budget Day.

"However, what I can say is, New Zealand's researchers make an extraordinary contribution and deserve a system that supports excellence and stability."

World.title: Wellington councillor still at loggerheads with mayor over search and rescue
World.content:
Photo: RNZ / Mark Papalii

A Wellington councillor who quit a sub-committee a week ago is still at loggerheads with the city mayor over his involvement at a search and rescue operation during Wellington's floods.

Wharangi/Onslow-Western Ward councillor Ray Chung resigned as chair of the Council Controlled Organisations subcommittee earlier this month.

Chung was at the search area for missing Karori man Philip Sutton on 21 April, who was swept away in floodwaters, after friends of Sutton's family issued a call for volunteers on a day police had suspended their search. Police later urged the public not to take the search into their own hands.

Mayor Andrew Little said Chung was told before he attended the scene that the search was a police matter. Ultimately, he should not have got involved in a search operation, Little said.

"Cr Chung told me he was being contacted by people who had concerns about the missing person search. I told him the search was a police matter. I told the councillor to contact the Police Area Commander."

A week on from his resignation, Chung maintains he was not getting involved in the search, and he stood by his actions.

He said he was only heading to the scene to try and prevent volunteers from getting in harm's way, after finding out members of the public were getting involved in the search.

He would not speak to why he resigned from the subcomittee.

"I absolutely wasn't getting involved in the search, the mayor knows it, the police know it.

"All I did, was I was doing what I think councillors should be doing, is looking after their constituents, when their constituents need help, you go and see what you can do to help them."

Chung sent an email, which RNZ has seen, in which he told council officers and the mayor he was going to the scene to try to stop people going into the water there.

Chung said he did not have the area commander's phone number, so he contacted a police officer from the search and rescue unit, who told him he did not want volunteers doing their own search, and asked Chung to tell them not to get involved.

Police have not confirmed that version of events.

Little said a senior member of police, Wellington Area Comander Dean Silvester, contacted him about Chung's involvement in the search - including "inappropriate contact" the councillor had made by speaking with the head of the search and rescue unit.

"He contacted me through text to say he was concerned about it, we had a conversation, I took those issues up with Ray, we had ongoing discussions. I have to say my priority at the time was getting council's response, sorting people out and getting rubbish collections and all that sort of stuff - and I did say it wouldn't be my top priority at the time."

Little said he later spoke with Chung, and "expressed a lack of confidence in him", and Chung subsequently chose to resign.

When asked why Chung's behaviour was concerning, Little said: "We were in a state of emergency, there was a search that the police had commenced but had suspended for safety reasons, and he along with others, had chosen to get involved and resume the search when it was contrary to the police's guidance and direction."

Little said the issue was over as far as he was concerned.

"That's it, from my point of view, to the extent I had concerns, the issue's now been disposed of, because he's no longer in a responsible role.

Wellington Area Commander Inspector Dean Silvester said he spoke with the mayor during the week of Wellington's severe weather, which is "normal in such an event".

"No complaint was made."

World.title: Can your employer force you to arrive early?
World.content:
Photo: Pexels

If you start work at 9am, can your employer require you to be there at five to?

A Sydney hair salon featured in Australian news coverage last week when the owner told staff they had to be punctual.

In a staff meeting posted on Tiktok, the owner, identified at Jessica Mina, told staff at Sheshwarz salon in Roselands that she hated when they walked in at the time they started.

"If you start at 9.30 or you start at 10 or you start at 12, be here ready to work at 12.

"I'm not asking you to come 20 minutes early but have your bag put down, your coffee put down and you're ready to start your 9.30 appointment."

Some commenters on the video asked whether staff would be paid for the time they were there getting ready.

Alison Maelzer, a partner at Hesketh Henry, said how this would be approached in New Zealand was not straightforward.

"Generally speaking, an employer can expect an employee to be at work, ready to commence work, at the agreed start time. Usually, there would be something in the employment agreement to that effect.

"However, if the employee needs to take particular actions or do things in order to be ready to start work - for example, setting up a hair stylist's station, or preparing a shop for opening by deactivating the security, logging in to the systems and preparing for trading - this becomes a bit more nuanced.

"Employees are entitled to be paid for the hours that they work. There are a number of cases that are authority for this proposition, including in relation to pre-work staff meetings, and travel to work locations. If the actions needed to prepare for trading, or get ready for a client's appointment are 'work', then the employee should usually be paid for that time.

"This might also apply to circumstances where extensive uniform or safety equipment is required to be put on at the start of the day and removed at the end of the day - the time spent 'gearing up' and then removing the equipment/uniform at the end of the day, will usually be considered work, and employees will often be paid an allowance for the time taken in these circumstances.

"Usually, employers and employees will take a pragmatic, practical approach. For example, it might be sensible for an employer to roster at least one retail employee to start earlier so that they can set up, ahead of the time the shop opens to the public. In the case of a hair salon, it would seem sensible to schedule the day's first appointment at a time shortly after the salon opens, so that everything is in order by the time the customer arrives - scheduling an appointment for the exact time the employees commence work does not seem like it would make for a good customer experience."

Workers First deputy secretary Rudd Hughes said unpaid pre-start expectations were common across many workplaces, in retail, hospitality, healthcare and trades.

"It tends to be far less prevalent where workers are unionised, because members know to raise it and unions treat it as a clear line.

"Most workers just absorb it quietly, which is exactly why employers get away with it.

"Ultimately, it's a form of wage theft. if your employer requires you to be somewhere and ready, that's work time."

Sheshwarz said staff were being paid for the time they were at work.

World.title: Kiwibank first to begin roll-out of open banking ahead of regulatory deadlines
World.content:
Photo: RNZ / Marika Khabazi

Kiwibank says it will become the first bank in New Zealand to fully roll out open banking to both individual and business customers.

From Thursday, customers will be able to securely share their banking data with approved third-party services, including budgeting apps, lenders and payment providers, through Kiwibank's internet banking and mobile app.

Open banking allows people and businesses to connect their bank accounts to other financial services, with customer consent, making it easier to manage money, make payments and access more personalised products through secure systems that allow services to share data.

Kiwibank said it was not intending to charge fintechs - who develop open banking applications - to access its systems.

Kiwibank chief customer officer Mark Stephen said the move was about giving customers more choice and helping foster innovation in the financial sector.

The bank was initially partnering with local fintech company Wych, to connect Kiwibank with accredited third parties securely.

It was also working with local fintechs Akahu and Volley to deliver open banking services, with plans to expand the number of providers as the system developed.

Stephen said the "open" in open banking reflects the potential for new services that did not yet exist - but that customers would be able to connect to them easily when they did.

Businesses were expected to be among the early adopters, with open banking tools offering the potential to automate processes, improve cashflow management and streamline payments and compliance.

Kiwibank said customers would remain in control of how their data is shared, and with whom, with consent underpinning every connection.

The rollout comes ahead of regulatory deadlines, as New Zealand's banking sector moves towards a more open data environment aimed at boosting competition and expanding the range of services available to consumers and businesses.

World.title: Young saviour and an answered prayer deliver Blues incredible Origin win
World.content:
When New South Wales found themselves in the depths of hell in State of Origin I, they looked to the heavens and asked for deliverance.

But they needn't have. The means of their salvation was within them the whole time, even as the scoreboard mounted and another Queensland ambush seemed to turn Stadium Australia into a cold and bloodless citadel.

In Ethan Strange and James Tedesco, they were gifted a young saviour and an answered prayer, and their efforts in the Blues' astounding 22-20 victory are the stuff of Origin legend.

They are two men at opposite ends of time. Strange is 21, and this was his New South Wales debut. It came on two days' notice, but that didn't matter. He plays like a hell-diver, fearless even at midnight in the belly of the beast, because he is too young ever to be afraid.

Tedesco is 33, the oldest player in the series, the Blues' living legend of these times. He is back after some time away, and he will do anything to make these days last a little bit longer.

They were not alone in pulling off the greatest comeback in Origin history or in resurrecting a cause that looked hopeless until Kalyn Ponga's send-off with 22 minutes remaining.

The Maroons were forced to finish with 12 players after Kalyn Ponga was sent off. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

The Blues don't win this game without Ponga's dismissal, and the advantage shook New South Wales out of the lethargy that had engulfed them through the opening hour.

Hudson Young, whose time in the Canberra chaos machine makes him no stranger to events that defy the laws of rugby league, had his best Origin match and was strong even before the flashpoint.

But for others, having something to target in the depleted Queenslanders brought out the killer in them.

Stephen Crichton, on a difficult night where errors plagued him, had his best Origin moment when he linked with Strange for the latter's second-half try.

Kotoni Staggs proved he is built for this land of wolves, acting as a hunter in attack and a punisher in defence, while Victor Radley played with blatant disregard for what would happen to him next.

And, of course, Nathan Cleary went some way to silencing those final doubters of his greatness with a final ten minutes where he returned to whatever plane of existence he found in the final minutes of the 2023 grand final against Brisbane.

The order of events was different, but the result — a try, a try assist and a 40/20 inside the final 15 minutes to help tear his team out of the grave — was the same.

Tedesco stunner completes greatest Origin comeback James Tedesco scores a spectacular try with 90 seconds left in State of Origin I, capping off a 20-point comeback after Queensland fullback Kalyn Ponga is sent off for a shoulder charge.

Cleary's ultimate Origin legacy will remain an endless fuel for the take furnace until this series is decided, but he would not have been in the position to bring the Blues home were it not for Strange. Cleary took them home, but Strange lit the way.

As Queensland stormed to their 20-0 lead, Strange threatened to join the legions of Origin debutants who blink and miss their maiden voyage in interstate football.

But his first big moment was also his state's — a hit on Cameron Munster forced Queensland's first error of the night after a perfect Maroon opening. Young scored soon thereafter, and the Blues had a pulse.

After the second half, the good stuff kept coming. It was Strange's pass that put Tolu Koula away down the sideline before Ponga's shoulder charge.

He had a try disallowed for obstruction, then scored one on a brilliant interchange of passing with Young and Crichton.

Strange slammed the ball into his own forehead afterwards, like he does when he scores big tries for the Raiders.

He himself isn't sure why he does that — it's just a little piece of madness that feels right.

As the half continued, Strange's running game came to the fore, and, with a state on his shoulders, he could carry the weight.

Strange wasn't perfect — he was penalised for a pass off the ground as the Blues were on the attack and searching for the winner — but nobody ever entered folklore by painting all the way inside the lines.

Tedesco calls upon experience

Tedesco wasn't perfect either. His bad pass forced an error from Haumole Olakau'atu when the tryline was begging in the second half, and had the Blues not won it, it would have been the edge of the knives being sharpened for him.

But Tedesco's superpower, the hallmark of his magnificent Origin career, is that he never stops moving and never stops going.

Harness his energy, distil his desire into fuel for the rest of us, and you'll solve the energy crisis. But it cannot belong to anyone else. It exists in him alone.

He was strong under the high ball all night, in attack and defence. Queensland went after him, but Tedesco kept finding the air up there, and even before his final try, his kick chase on Cleary's bombs had drawn two penalties and forced several errors from the Maroons back three.

It took every bit of Tedesco's desire and Strange's hunger to bring the Blues home, and plenty of other things besides. This comeback is inextricably linked to Ponga's send-off, and that is the hinge on which the game swung.

James Tedesco scored the match-winning try in the shadows of full-time. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

But it had to swing on something, and when they chalk it up in the history books, there are no asterisks or explainers, just the score, carved out of blood and bone.

There is still much to be done in this series and perhaps further legends to be made.

The Blues will not get a second chance like this again if they don't start stronger in Melbourne.

Queensland are in the kind of hurt that you only hear about in sad country songs, but they are always at their most dangerous when badly wounded.

They will rightly feel like, were it not for the Ponga send-off, they would have gotten home handily, and it creates a fascinating dynamic for the MCG in a few weeks.

But that's a problem for the future, and this was a classic, the kind the game was crying out for, and that's worth breathing in. Tedesco has had so many great Origin moments and, judging from this game, Strange will have many more to come.

On this night, they collided in history, past and future incarnate, and brought their team back. But it wasn't a resurrection because the Blues were buried alive until Strange and Tedesco dug them up.

World.title: FIFA faces investigation over 'impossibly high' World Cup ticket prices
World.content:
The attorneys-general of New York and New Jersey say they will investigate soaring ticket prices and allegations of misleading seat locations for the upcoming 2026 FIFA World Cup tournament.

In a joint statement, New Jersey Attorney General Jennifer Davenport and New York Attorney General Letitia James said they had issued subpoenas to FIFA, requesting information about the sporting body's ticket practices.

This year's FIFA World Cup is being held across North America, with the tournament's final among eight games being hosted by New Jersey.

The joint statement said they had requested FIFA outline how it had come to charge for, and select, seats for fans at all eight of those games.

It came amid allegations from some ticket-buyers that they had been misled about the location of the seats they purchased.

The FIFA World Cup, which is being played across the US, Canada and Mexico, kicks off from mid-June. (Reuters: Ed Ou)

The attorneys-general accused FIFA of having changed the "category" of tickets they had purchased after the fact, altering seat map divisions and creating new zones for more in-demand seats after some tickets had already been sold.

In some instances, fans alleged the category of their seats had been changed to move them further back from the field than initially believed.

'Fake scarcity'

The investigations would also look into whether FIFA's use of "variable pricing" had caused the cost of tickets to skyrocket.

Fans had been reporting seeing tickets being offered for in excess of $US1,000 ($1,400) in some instances, which the joint statement from Ms James and Ms Davenport said was far higher than what had been charged at any prior to the FIFA World Cup.

In one instance, FIFA released tickets to a match between the US and Paraguay costing $US4,105.

FIFA provides more expensive World Cup tickets After a backlash over ticket prices, FIFA puts up a new option for fans — and it is more expensive.

“No one should be manipulated into paying sky-high prices for seats, and fans should be able to trust that the tickets they purchase will be the ones they receive," Ms James said.

Ms Davenport accused the football governing body of having turned "buying a ticket to the World Cup into a gauntlet of confusion, fake scarcity, and impossibly high prices".

FIFA has previously defended its pricing as indicative of high public demand.

The upcoming competition has been marred by various scandals, including accusations a transit company in New Jersey had upped train ticket prices on game days to over $US100 for journeys that normally would cost $US10.

FIFA declined to comment on this latest investigation, according to Reuters.

Speaking last year, the World Cup's chief operating officer Heimo Schirgi said sales of tickets were a vital revenue stream to fulfil FIFA's objective of "providing funding, providing opportunities, providing growth to our sport across all the 211 member associations".

"And as part of that mission, which we take very seriously, we’re looking at optimising the revenue, but also optimising attendance in the stadium, right? So, it’s always a balance between different factors."

ABC/AP

World.title: Kalyn Ponga's Origin send-off leaves Queensland legend 'in shock'
World.content:
Origin greats have been left "in shock" by the decision to send Kalyn Ponga off in State of Origin I, opening the door for NSW's miraculous comeback at Homebush.

Former Maroons captain Darren Lockyer said it was undeniably "the turning point" in the match and a bitter pill to swallow, arguing on-field referee Ashley Klein overruled the bunker to dismiss Ponga for the rest of the game rather than sending him to the sin-bin or 10 minutes.

"I'm still in shock about the Kalyn Ponga decision," the veteran of 36 Origin matches said on Channel Nine after the Blues' 22-20 victory in Sydney.

"That's the turning point; we lose the game off the back of that. There'll be a lot of people north of the border that struggle to accept that decision."

Ponga became the seventh man sent off in Origin. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

The Blues were surging but Queensland still led 20-6 when Tolu Koula broke down the left wing with 23 minutes left in the series opener.

Halfback Sam Walker came across the field to drag him down, with Koula angling his body to get to ground and away from the sideline as he came to the Queensland fullback.

Both players dropped low and Ponga tucked his left arm in a classic shoulder charge position, making dramatic contact with Koula, which replays showed was a brutal head clash.

Loading Instagram content

As Koula lay sprawled on the turf with a cut on his eyebrow, players came together for some jersey grabbing, and pushing and shoving.

Ponga cut a miserable figure, knowing he was in serious trouble, while Blues lock Cameron Murray was heard telling Klein to remember NSW star Joseph Suaalii was sent off in the 2024 series opener for a completely different high shot on Reece Walsh.

Klein immediately was heard saying "I'm thinking that's a send-off", before an apparent disagreement with bunker official Chris Butler about the severity of the punishment.

Referee Ashley Klein overruled bunker official Chris Butler. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

"He's hit him directly in the head," Klein said before listening to a response from the video referee.

"I get that mate, but this is in the head, there's no attempt to tackle," he said into his earpiece.

Another pause before calling Ponga over …

"I know what you're saying, but this is an illegal play," he added before sending Ponga for an early shower as the Newcastle superstar pointed to blood on his ear as evidence of the head clash.

Origin greats Andrew Johns and Cameron Smith were outraged in the Channel Nine commentary box.

"It's not a send-off," ex-Queensland skipper Cameron Smith said.

Ponga became the seventh man sent off in Origin. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

"No way it's a send-off," Immortal Andrew Johns replied.

Lockyer was unimpressed by Klein apparently overruling Butler.

"I think Ashley Klein always had this [the send off] in his mind," he said after the game.

"The bunker said it should be 10 minutes … but Ashley Klein didn't have a bar of it."

Maroons coach Billy Slater said after the game that he was OK with the decision.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"I haven't got any problems with it," he told reporters.

"I'm not gonna make any noise about it. They're the breaks."

NSW coach Laurie Daley initially said he would "rather not say" what he thought of the incident, before suggesting it was the sort of thing that had happened plenty of times in Origin before (i.e. one side benefiting massively from a tough call).

"If you look through Origin history there's always been moments and there's always been wins like that," he said.

"You take 'em."

The match review committee hit Ponga with a grade-two shoulder charge, which would be worth a two-match ban with an early guilty plea had it happened in an NRL game.

But, under rules introduced in 2022 to stop players missing club matches for offences committed while on representative duty, he will instead be fined 23 per cent of his match fee with an early plea.

World.title: Quick hits: Blues' selection gamble pays off, bunker sparks controversy
World.content:
The Blues leave it late to win State of Origin I 22-20, the Maroons finish with 12 players, while the bunker draws the ire of players, commentators and spectators alike.

Here are five quick hits from Origin I at Sydney's Stadium Australia.

1. Tedesco repays Daley's faith

Cometh the hour, cometh James Tedesco.

With the Maroons leading 20-16 with just 90 seconds left in the match, the Blues had no choice but to roll the dice after blowing some excellent scoring opportunities.

From 31 metres out, Nathan Cleary went to the sky with a high ball, as Tedesco chased through for a one-on-one contest with Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow.

Tedesco won the ball in the air close to the Maroons' line, but the drama did not end there.

The former Blues skipper bobbled the ball before grounding over the line to level the score at 20-20.

The Blues still needed to land the conversion to secure the win, with Cleary in charge of goal-kicking duties.

After the clock stopped with five seconds left, Cleary sent the crowd into a frenzy when he coolly landed the decisive two points.

It capped off a remarkable comeback, with the Blues trailing 20-6 as late as the 62nd minute.

Tedesco was a contentious selection, with Blues coach Laurie Daley opting for the Roosters custodian over incumbent Dylan Edwards.

2. Ponga given marching orders

Holding a 14-point lead, 17 minutes into the second half, it appeared the Maroons were headed for a comfortable win.

That was when the match turned on its head.

Blues winger Tolutau Koula was steaming down the left touchline, with Kalyn Ponga coming across in cover defence.

Ponga helped Sam Walker stop Koula in his tracks, but his shoulder made contact with the head of the Blues debutant.

Kalyn Ponga (left) is sent from the field by referee Ashley Klein. (AAP: Mark Evans)

A scuffle between the two teams ensued but once the dust settled, referee Ashley Klein called out Ponga and delivered the news no Maroons supporter wanted to hear.

"It's a shoulder charge, you're off," Klein told a bewildered Ponga, who attempted to plead his case.

Ponga's send-off was judged extreme by the Nine TV commentary team.

"It's a sin-bin," Andrew Johns said.

Koula did not appear again in the match, having left the field before failing an HIA.

The Maroons were forced to finish the match with 12 players, allowing the Blues to launch their fightback.

3. Bunker denies Blues try

Were the Blues robbed in the first half?

In the 36th minute, Cameron Murray appeared to have scored a try after chasing through on Reece Robson's kick, which had bounced off the posts into the in-goal area.

Murray beat Kurt Capewell to the ball but almost lost control it before grounding for what would have been the Blues' second try.

Cameron Murray (right) was penalised for interfering with Kurt Capewell. (Nine Network)

Klein, however, referred the play to the bunker, who claimed Murray was "playing the man", that being Capewell, and gave the Maroons a penalty.

"There's not much in it but as soon as he places hands on Capewell's back, that's what they look for," Maroons great Cameron Smith said on Nine's coverage.

Murray was ready to celebrate, as was the parochial Blues crowd.

It would have been a regulation conversion attempt had the try been awarded, given the proximity to the posts, which would have set up a 20-12 scoreline in the Maroons' advantage.

Instead, the Maroons took a 20-6 lead into the half-time break.

4. Solid Origin debuts

Several players were making their Origin debuts, but Ethan Strange was perhaps the most impressive.

A late inclusion for the Blues following Mitchell Moses's injury, Strange stood tall, scoring the try that kick-started the host's fightback following Ponga's send-off.

He was penalised late in the match when the Blues were on the attack, but it was an otherwise blemish-free debut from the Canberra Raiders star.

For the Maroons, any fears Sam Walker would be feeling nerves in his Origin debut abated early in the first half.

In one of his first touches, Walker set up Robert Toia for the opening try of the match in the 10th minute.

Deep inside Blues' territory, the Maroons went right from dummy half through Harry Grant, who found Walker at first receiver.

The Maroons halfback took the ball to the line and stabbed a kick behind the oncoming Blues defenders, as Toia sprinted through to touch down for his try.

Only four minutes later, Walker threw the final pass to Tom Flegler for the Maroons' second try of the match.

5. Maroons honour 'brother' Arrow

Jai Arrow travelled with the Maroons squad to Stadium Australia. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

The news Jai Arrow had been diagnosed with MND rocked the rugby league world last week.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Arrow made 12 Origin appearances for the Maroons during his career, which was tragically cut short following his diagnosis.

The 30-year-old spent time with the Maroons in camp before Origin I and travelled with the squad on their bus to Stadium Australia on Wednesday evening.

Arrow was named the Maroons' honorary 21st man, with a jersey bearing his name hanging up in the sheds before the match.

"Tonight we play for our brother," a Maroons' Instagram post read.

Loading Instagram content

The Maroons' touching gesture is the latest example of the NRL community uniting behind Arrow.

North Queensland fans raised $50,000 for MND charities during their match with South Sydney on Sunday, when organisers sold a record $100,847 worth of raffle tickets.

World.title: Maroons let 20-0 lead slip in Origin I after Kalyn Ponga sent off late
World.content:
James Tedesco has scored a spectacular try with 90 seconds left in State of Origin I to cap off a stunning comeback to win State of Origin I 22-20 at a sodden Stadium Australia.

An electric Queensland outfit shot out to a 20-0 lead after 20 minutes of the series opener in Sydney, before spending an hour desperately trying to cling on.

That task was made harder when superstar fullback Kalyn Ponga was sent off for a shoulder charge on a flying Tolu Koula after 57 minutes.

Loading Instagram content

Cameron Munster and Ponga insisted that it was the fullback's head, not his shoulder, that hit Koula high.

But Ashley Klein would not be moved, noting Ponga's shoulder-charge action before making the Newcastle fullback the seventh man to be sent off in an Origin match, although not everyone agreed.

"I'm still in shock about the Kalyn Ponga decision," Queensland legend Darren Lockyer said on Channel Nine after the game.

Kalyn Ponga had played a sensational game until his blunder. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

"Credit to New South Wales, but there will be plenty of people north of the border who will struggle to accept that decision."

The score at that stage was 20-6 for Queensland but the send off completely changed the complexion of the contest.

Debutant Ethan Strange and halfback Nathan Cleary scored on 62 and 71 minutes, as the Maroons' defence scrambled in the wet.

They repelled the Blues until the final moments, when Cleary's bomb landed a metre in front of the tryline and Tedesco outleapt Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow, pinched the ball, juggled and regathered on the way to grounding.

James Tedesco scored a miracle try in the final 90 seconds to win the game for the Blues. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

"That was unreal, a bit surreal to be honest," Tedesco, the reigning Dally M medallist who was playing his first Origin match since Game I of 2024.

"We dug deep, we knew we'd get some opportunities.

"We made too many errors [in the first half] … we made it hard for ourselves.

"We had plenty of opportunities and I'm just glad I came up with something."

Cleary potted the extras from just next to the posts and NSW took a 1-0 series lead before the series heads to Melbourne for Game II in three weeks' time.

The Blues will celebrate tonight, but will be left wondering how Queensland got such a jump on them in the opening exchanges.

Uncharacteristic errors from Brian To'o and Stephen Crichton didn't help the Blues, but the Maroons were utterly irresistible for the first half hour of the game.

Tom Flegler was swarmed by his teammates after scoring a try in his return to the Origin arena. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Robert Toia, Thomas Flegler and Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow all scored in the opening 16 minutes of the match, with Sam Walker playing brilliantly on debut, kicking four goals from four.

But the Blues scored off their very first foray into the Maroons end, Hudson Young scoring off a magical kick by Nathan Cleary, who was later awarded player of the match honours.

They Blues could have had a second before the break only for Cameron Murray to be penalised for a foul before grounding in the in-goal.

The game evolved into an arm wrestle early in the second half, before Ponga's crucial collision, which resulted in Koula being subbed out of the game with a concussion and Ponga fined 23 per cent of his match fee.

Look back on how all the action unfolded in our live blog.

Live updates State of Origin Game I S By Simon Smale Collapse all posts off Sort Sort posts Latest Select an option New: Filters Choose what information you see below by using filters Filter Posts All 124 Key Events 19 Tries 7 Goals 1 Comments 12 All filters Time to say goodbye S By Simon Smale (Getty Images) Well, a stunning victory for the Blues, as dramatic as it could possibly be, with the people's champion James Tedesco scoring the winner on his return to the Origin stage. Genuinely couldn't happen to a nicer guy. As far as Queensland will be concerned, that was one that got away. To be 20-0 up and still lose the game, no matter the circumstances, is a failure and puts the defending champions on the back foot heading to the MCG next month. Was the Ponga send off correct? I think it depends on who you are talking to. The fact is that Tolu Koula was unable to resume the match after the incident due to the contact. There is also, from the alternative side, that Ashley Klein overruled the Bunker official who told him the incident did not meet the threshold for a send off. That conversation will rumble on and on. But, for now, our conversation is over. Thanks so much for being with us on a soggy night in capitals either side of the border. Until we meet again, at the MCG on June 17. 'The Blues don't win that game unless Ponga gets sent off': Paul Gallen S By Simon Smale Paul Gallen is speaking on Channel Nine at the moment. He is pretty adamant that the Blues were the second best team on the ground throughout the opening exchanges. He says that the Blues may even need to make a couple of changes ahead of the second game. "The Blues don't win that game unless Ponga gets sent off," Ponga says. "I think they need to keep a lid on it and pick a team that can win Game II because you do not want to go up to Queensland for a decider." Murray credits Blues pressure S By Simon Smale Cameron Murray is speaking now to Channel Nine. He still looks to be in a bit of shock about how the game was turned around so late. He is asked about what the Blues did well when the Maroons were down to 12 men, and he says that it was basically just their pressure. "We probably just did a great job with building pressure," Murray says. "We just put a bit more fatigue in their defensive line." They sure did - the Blues dominated late on, at one stage earning seven sets in a row against the Maroons increasingly desperate defence. Daley won't be drawn on the Ponga decision J By Jon Healy The NSW coach is asked about Kalyn Ponga being sent off the field. "I'd rather not say," he says. I'll leave it to you to decipher that. Does he want to avoid being panned for kicking a bloke when he's down or did he disagree with the call? I think more likely the former, but he's not given us much to go off. Captain Isaah Yeo says he thinks it was a send-off, but admits he's hardly an impartial observer. "Bias says I think it's a send off. We've been on that side of it as well. I don't know." Daley says this is nothing new. "If you look through Origin history there's always been moment and there's always been wins like that; you take 'em." Slater's pride J By Jon Healy Slater pretty much always talks about being proud of his team, but you can tell there's a little more feeling behind it tonight. "We've gotta take some positives out of what we did tonight, and there were a lot. "It's natural to feel heartbroken and disappointed but we won't be throwing the baby out with the bath water." The coach is asked what he's most proud of. "The heart and spirit they fought with. "Twenty-three minutes in a State of Origin game with 12 men, they fought hard. You could see they were just holding on in stages. "One moment at the end of the game it could be a different story, but it's not. "I'm sure all Queenslanders are proud of their footy team right now." 'I suggest you ask someone else': Gould refuses to talk about send off S By Simon Smale The Channel Nine team are talking about the send off. There are mixed feelings. "We could hear the thump [sideline]," Darren Lockyer says. "I looks sickening from a distance. "And I think Ashley Klein always had this [the send off] in his mind. "The Bunker said it should be 10 minutes ... but Ashley Klein didn't have a bar of it." Brad Fittler is more accepting of the call. "As the defender, you have responsibility ... you have to be on the down side," Fittler says. "That's why he was sent off." As for what Gus Gould thinks? He pleads the fifth. "I suggest you ask someone else, not me," Gus Gould says. Interesting. "He's probably thinking he's cost the team the game," Lockyer says. "There will be a lot of people in the changing room at the moment, who will be perplexed at how that happened." Billy Slater has no problems with Kalyn Ponga send-off J By Jon Healy Queensland coach Billy Slater says the decision to send Kalyn Ponga off "is what it is". "I haven't got any problems with it. "I'm not gonna make any noise about it. They're the breaks." He says Ponga "obviously feels like he let his team down". Captain Cameron Munster says he felt like the speed of the incident and the fact Ponga tried to get low with Tolu Koula, plus the head-to-head contact, might have meant it was only a sin-bin. "I thought it might have been head on head but the ref and the bunker saw it differently. Those are the rules. Ref's gotta make a split decision." Strange 'sparked' the Blues: Johns S By Simon Smale Andrew Johns says Ethan Strange "sparked" the Blues. "You're looking at a guy who may play 30 Origins," he says. "After KP got sent off and the field opened up, he was "devastating Cameron Smith agrees. "I agree," he says.

"It was a wonderful debut." Darren Lockyer 'in shock' over Ponga send off S By Simon Smale Here is Queensland legend Darren Lockyer. He is very, very unhappy. "I'm still in shock about the Kalyn Ponga decision," he says. "Credit to New South Wales, but there will be plenty of people north of the border who will struggle to accept that decision." Young 'proud' of Strange S By Simon Smale Hudson Young is being interviewed now on Nine. "I am so proud of Ethan," he says. :First time he stepped on the field you knew he would be an Origin player, and he stepped up tonight." Gould: 'The first 25 minutes was everything I feared' S By Simon Smale "The first 25 minutes was everything I feared," says Gus Gould on Nine. "They started the second half pretty positively. "There was some really magical individual moments. I don't want playing against 12 men to take away from what he [Nathan Cleary] did under very difficult conditions. 'Greatest' Origin comeback ever? S By Simon Smale How can the NSW origin win be called the greatest come back win, when NSW played against 10 men for the greater part of the 2nd half? Poor decision by the referee against the spirit of state of origin rugby, that may set a precedent for future origin games. Ridiculous call! - Victorian Dale Not sure you can call it the “greatest origin comeback” when it’s a home game and 13 vs 12…. - Lj The blues played terribly for a team that was a man up for a quarter of the game. When Ponga went off I was expecting a blow out - Josh So NSW can win an Origin! (Against 12) - Muzz 'A different level': Haumole Olakau'atu S By Simon Smale Haumole Olakau'atu is speaking to ABC Sport too. He could have won the game much earlier for the Blues only to drop the ball with a three-man overlap. "I should've caught that but as I bent over to catch the ball everything just locked up and that was my night," he says. "Bad pass or not you still gotta execute and it wasn't good enough from my end. "I'm just glad Tedesco did that. If it was anyone else I don't know whether they would've pulled it off. "All these talks about the speed of the game is next level and it was no joke. This … is a different level." 'They're a hard enough team to defend when you've got a full team': Capewell S By Simon Smale (@ABCSport) Kurt Capewell has been speaking to ABC Sport too. "Definitely disappointing. We set the game up well and to lose like that hurts, but that's footy," he says. "They're a hard enough team to defend when you've got a full team out there, let alone 12 men. "We'll learn from it." To quote Nathan Cleary, 'Origin, hey?' S By Simon Smale One of the great Origins. Not a perfect performance - probably one of the worst from a winning side in Origin - but holy hell what a ride. - Tom Tedesco: 'Nath ... was instrumental' S By Simon Smale (@ABCSport) Here's some more from James Tedesco, speaking to ABC Sport. "That was unreal, a bit surreal to be honest," he says. "We dug deep, we knew we'd get some opportunities. I bombed one earlier so I knew I had to make up for it. "We made too many errors [in the first half], it was very slippery, we made it hard for ourselves in the first half. "We had plenty of opportunities and I'm just glad I came up with something. "Nath put it on the spot. He was instrumental. Strangey was unreal." Sam Walker doesn't want to talk S By Simon Smale Sam Walker is speaking now. He doesn't want to but is being told he has to as the Channel Nine cameras pursue him across the Sydney turf. "It's a hard one to reflect on right now," he says. "Just disappointed I guess. "It's really special to be able to put the jersey on," he adds, looking anything but happy. 'It's just Origin, hey?' Nathan Cleary is man of the match S By Simon Smale Nathan Cleary sums up most of our thoughts about that game. "It's just Origin, hey?" he says. "Queensland got the jump on us, but a lot of the talk behind the line was really positive. "Obviously pretty disappointed with that first half, not much defensive resilience." Ethan Strange 'that was pretty special' S By Simon Smale Ethan Strange is speaking now. "That was pretty special that one," he says. "Playing with all these guys, they're legends of the game. "How about Nathan Cleary? "The way he manages the game is incredible." He says it was a blur of a match. He genuinely looks stunned to be out there still, living his dream. Show more posts
